title: Barcelona not expected to enter a bidding war to retain the services of PSG, Atletico target
description: As we enter the month of August, it is going to be a critical one as far as the future of Ferran Torres is concerned. The Spanish international’s contract at Camp Nou expires at the end of next seas...
fullText:
As we enter the month of August, it is going to be a critical one as far as the future of Ferran Torres is concerned.

The Spanish international’s contract at Camp Nou expires at the end of next season and has found himself on the radar of PSG and Atletico Madrid, with the former, in particular, in pole position to sign the forward.

Recent reports have indicated that Ferran is keen on a move to PSG although Barcelona are actively trying to offer him a renewal in order to retain his services.

Ferran Torres’ future hangs in the balance. (Photo by Diego Souto/Getty Images)

According to Diario SPORT, Barcelona are refusing to enter into a financial bidding war for the striker.

The club intend to present him with a renewal proposal in line with their salary policy, effective from September, but that offer will not be improved to fend off outside interest.

Should Ferran opt to pursue one of the proposals on his table, with PSG leading the way, Barcelona will not enhance the terms and would instead look to negotiate his exit for a fair fee.

The club want to keep Ferran, viewing him as a valued member of the squad with excellent attacking qualities and a good goalscoring record, but they will not lose their heads over him. As the club see it, no player is truly indispensable.

Ultimately, the ball is in Ferran’s court. Barcelona are still in the dark regarding PSG and have had little contact with the player’s camp, learning of the interest largely through the media.

It must now be Ferran himself who steps forward to confirm whether he wishes to stay or asks to leave.

Barcelona won’t be desperate to keep hold of Ferran. (Photo by David Ramos/Getty Images)

Ferran’s decision could have significant knock-on effects for the rest of Barcelona’s attacking plans, particularly their pursuit of Julian Alvarez.

Should Ferran depart, Barcelona would be left without a recognised centre-forward in the squad, save for the emerging Hamza Abdelkarim.

That would only intensify Hansi Flick’s calls for a new number nine in what is proving an extremely difficult market for strikers.

In that sense, Ferran’s future is intrinsically linked to how aggressively Barcelona push for Alvarez. His exit would make signing a striker an absolute necessity rather than a luxury, adding further urgency to a pursuit that has already been complicated by Atletico’s firm stance.

Should he leave, Barcelona would at least hope to recoup the €55 million they paid to sign him from the Premier League, funds that could then be reinvested in solving their ongoing search for a forward.

For now, though, the club await Ferran’s decision.

title: Bears' Jaylon Johnson: Caleb Williams is the best quarterback I've had since Nick Foles
description: Johnson may have damned Williams with faint praise in suggesting that Williams is not the Bears' best quarterback during Johnson's seven years in Chicago.
fullText:
Chicago cornerback Jaylon Johnson has been with the Bears since they drafted him in 2020, and he's faced a lot of quarterbacks on the practice field during that time. Perhaps surprisingly, he doesn't necessarily view Caleb Williams as the best of those quarterbacks.

In what might be considered damning with faint praise, Johnson talked up the Bears' offense when asked about training camp practices, but he suggested that Williams isn't the best Bears quarterback he's practiced against, just the best since Nick Foles was in Chicago during Johnson's first two seasons.

"Honestly, this is probably the best offense I've had in seven years, as far as going against them, for sure. They've got a lot of speed," Johnson said. "Caleb's the best quarterback I've had, again, since I feel like maybe Nick Foles, if you want to go back that far. Just as far as slinging it, I feel like he's definitely doing his thing, you can see the accuracy, you can see the confidence, throwing the ball in tight windows is something that's stood out to me. Top to bottom they're a confident group. They believe in each other, believe in what they're doing. That's what we need to go against on defense. They know what we're doing, they challenge us, we go after them, it's going to be a fun camp."

Foles had some stellar moments in his NFL career, making the Pro Bowl in his first season as the Eagles' primary starter in 2013, and winning Super Bowl MVP for the Eagles after the 2017 season. But that's not the Foles Johnson practiced against. Johnson was comparing Williams to the Foles who spent two years in Chicago late in his career, primarily as a backup to Mitchell Trubisky, Andy Dalton and Justin Fields.

That makes it a strange comparison. The Bears only won three games started by Foles during his two seasons as Johnson's teammate. The Bears won 11 games in the regular season and one in the playoffs last year. That apparently isn't enough for Johnson to declare Williams the best quarterback he's practiced against in Chicago, without exception.

title: Arteta coy on Vinicius Jr but says Arsenal very ambitious
description: Mikel Arteta refused to be drawn on speculation linking Arsenal with Real Madrid winger Vinicius Junior but insisted the Premier League champions remain ambitious as they continue to strengthen their ...
fullText:
Mikel Arteta refused to be drawn on speculation linking Arsenal with Real Madrid winger Vinicius Junior but insisted the Premier League champions remain ambitious as they continue to strengthen their squad.

The Arsenal manager was asked about the club’s transfer plans after Saturday’s 4-1 pre-season victory over Girona, where he made it clear that more business is expected before the window closes.

“Well, we are really active, trying to improve and evolve the team. That’s clear,” Arteta said.

“We expect to have movements in the next few weeks, obviously, because we want to get better like anybody else. And you can just see the transfer market and our opponents.

“What we are doing, we won’t sit still, and we are very ambitious in what we want to do.”

Arteta’s comments come amid continued speculation over Vinicius’ future at Real Madrid.

Arteta brushes off Vinicius Jr reports but says Arsenal ‘very ambitious’

Although Arsenal are understood to be monitoring the Brazil international’s contractual situation, Sky Sports News reports that the Spanish giants have no intention of selling the 26-year-old and remain confident he will sign a new long-term deal.

Vinicius has entered the final year of his current contract, prompting interest from several clubs, but Real Madrid continue to regard him as a key part of their long-term project.

Arteta was later asked, in a light-hearted exchange, when Vinicius would be arriving at the Emirates Stadium. The Spaniard responded with a smile before walking away without addressing the question.

Arsenal have made only two senior additions so far this summer, signing Christos Tzolis and Illan Meslier, but Arteta’s latest comments suggest further arrivals remain a priority as the club prepare to defend their Premier League title and challenge on multiple fronts.

While the Arsenal boss offered no indication that a move for Vinicius is imminent, he left little doubt that the club intend to remain active in the market over the coming weeks.

title: Dowman shines as Arsenal beat Girona in pre-season
description: Max Dowman stole the show as Arsenal opened their pre-season campaign with a convincing 4-1 victory over Girona, producing a goal and an assist in an eye-catching display.The highly rated midfielder p...
fullText:
Max Dowman stole the show as Arsenal opened their pre-season campaign with a convincing 4-1 victory over Girona, producing a goal and an assist in an eye-catching display.

The highly rated midfielder played a key role in two first-half goals, first threading an incisive pass through to Kai Havertz, who calmly slotted past Paulo Gazzaniga to open the scoring after 16 minutes.

Arsenal doubled their advantage midway through the first half when summer signing Christos Tzolis marked his debut with a goal. The Greece international skipped past Arnau Martinez before drilling a low effort into the bottom corner via a slight deflection to give Mikel Arteta’s side a deserved cushion.

Girona reduced the deficit four minutes after the restart as Martinez rose highest to head home from a corner, but Arsenal responded immediately through the impressive Dowman.

Dowman shines as Arsenal beat Girona in pre-season

The teenager restored the Gunners’ two-goal advantage just three minutes later with a composed finish before Gabriel Jesus completed a devastating five-minute spell by adding Arsenal’s fourth goal to put the result beyond doubt.

Arteta fielded a strong starting side in Spain, with Viktor Gyokeres, Havertz and Piero Hincapie all featuring for 30 minutes after returning from the World Cup. However, it was Dowman who emerged as the standout performer, underlining why he is regarded as one of the brightest talents to come through Arsenal’s academy in recent years.

Tzolis also made an encouraging first impression following his move from Club Brugge, while Jesus added another positive moment as Arsenal continued to build fitness ahead of the new campaign.

The Gunners now turn their attention to their second pre-season fixture, when they face Real Betis in Dublin on 5 August.

Bruno Guimaraes was expected to join Newcastle United’s preseason camp in La Manga on Friday, then Sunday, after receiving an extended break following Brazil’s World Cup campaign.

However, that reunion with his teammates and new head coach Matthias Jaissle may never happen.

The midfielder is seemingly trying to avoid the trip to Spain altogether as his proposed transfer to Arsenal moves toward completion. That’s according to TEAMtalk, which reported on Saturday night that Guimaraes and his representatives want him to fly directly to Arsenal’s HQ in London for a medical rather than report back to Newcastle.

“Bruno Guimaraes is hoping that he will not have to fly out to Spain on Sunday to link up with Newcastle United, with the Brazil international increasingly confident his move to Arsenal will be finalised before then,” TEAMtalk’s Graeme Bailey reported. “For Guimaraes the immediate focus remains on avoiding the flight to Spain altogether.”

The report confirmed earlier information revealing that Arsenal and Newcastle are now negotiating directly over a package worth more than £80 million, with the 28-year-old already agreeing a five-year contract.

“The transfer is now at such an advanced stage that those close to Guimaraes believe it would make far more sense for the midfielder to fly to London for his medical rather than travel to Newcastle’s pre-season base in La Manga,” Bailey reported.

Newcastle media keeps reporting the club expects its captain to report on Sunday, but Brunos’ representatives are pushing for the remaining details to be resolved beforehand and the deal could happen early Sunday and put an end to the saga.

The Times has also reported Arsenal agreed an £80 million package consisting of £70 million guaranteed and £10 million in add-ons, with Guimaraes scheduled to undergo a medical on Monday.

Everton have reached an agreement with Arsenal to sign Christian Norgaard in a deal worth £7 million, with the experienced midfielder now closing in on a move to the Merseyside club.

Norgaard is poised to become the club’s fourth signing of the summer as Everton continue to reshape their squad ahead of the new season. Hayden Hackney arrived earlier in a deal worth around £24m, while Tyrique George and Merlin Rohl also completed permanent moves to Merseyside.

For Arsenal, Norgaard’s departure would further streamline a midfield that already boasts strong competition for places. Although the Dane was valued for his leadership and experience, opportunities proved limited during his only season in north London.

Everton, meanwhile, believe the midfielder’s Premier League pedigree can help fill the void left by Gueye’s exit. Norgaard spent six seasons at Brentford before joining Arsenal and has built a reputation as a reliable defensive midfielder with strong positional awareness and leadership qualities.

The deal is now expected to progress towards completion, with Norgaard on the verge of becoming Everton’s latest addition before the start of the new Premier League campaign.

title: Report: Potential Arsenal move excites Aston Villa star
description: Ezri Konsa Transfer Latest: Arsenal Weigh Move as Liverpool Monitor SituationArsenal’s search for defensive reinforcement appears to be gathering pace, with Ezri Konsa emerging as one of the most cr...
fullText:
Arsenal’s search for defensive reinforcement appears to be gathering pace, with Ezri Konsa emerging as one of the most credible names under consideration ahead of the summer window. According to Caught Offside, the Aston Villa defender is on the radar of both Arsenal and Liverpool, with the report indicating he would be “interested” in a switch to the Emirates Stadium.

The key issue, as things stand, is valuation. Villa are understood to want £60m for the England international, a figure that may prove difficult for Arsenal to meet without significant internal conviction that Konsa is the right fit. The interest is real, but so too is the sense that the asking price could yet become a major obstacle.

Arsenal’s thinking is clear enough. William Saliba’s injury has sharpened the need for reliable central defensive cover, particularly with the new season approaching and little margin for disruption at the back. Saliba has become one of the side’s defining players, and any prolonged absence inevitably alters recruitment priorities.

In that context, Konsa makes sense. He is Premier League proven, tactically flexible and experienced at a high level. He would not arrive as a developmental project, but as a player capable of contributing immediately. That profile naturally carries appeal for a club trying to protect standards while navigating a demanding schedule.

There are, however, alternatives in the frame. Konstantinos Mavropanos has been mentioned as a lower-cost option after West Ham’s relegation to the Championship, while Como defender Jacobo Ramon is viewed more as a longer-term investment. Each presents a different type of opportunity, which suggests Arsenal are still weighing immediate readiness against broader squad planning.

Liverpool’s presence in the background is worth noting, even if the strongest indication at present points towards Arsenal as the more natural destination. Konsa is reportedly open to a move away from Villa Park, though there is no indication he is agitating for an exit. That keeps control firmly with Aston Villa, who can afford to be patient unless the market shifts in a meaningful way.

From Arsenal’s perspective, this increasingly feels like a decision over price and priority. Konsa offers assurance, familiarity with the league and the sort of consistency recruitment teams tend to value highly. The question is whether that package is enough to justify £60m, particularly when other defensive names remain under active consideration.

From an intrigued Arsenal supporter’s point of view, this report is easy to understand. Konsa feels like one of those signings who may not generate huge noise at first, but could quickly look very sensible once the season gets going. He knows the Premier League, he is dependable, and he would reduce the anxiety around losing Saliba for any meaningful stretch.

The concern, naturally, is the £60m fee. That is serious money for a player who probably comes in as cover initially, even if he would play plenty. Arsenal have to be smart here because there are multiple areas of the squad that may need attention, and overcommitting on one position can create issues elsewhere.

Even so, there is a strong logic to this. The squad already has versatile defenders, but there is a difference between emergency cover and a specialist centre-back you trust in major matches. Konsa looks much closer to the latter. If Arsenal believe he can slot in quickly and maintain the level expected, then the interest is understandable.

Supporters will probably be split between wanting a cheaper option and wanting certainty. Right now, certainty feels valuable. If the price can be nudged down, this could become one of the more sensible moves of the summer.

title: Liverpool boss full of praise for youthful stars on US pre-season tour
description: Andoni Iraola’s Liverpool USA Tour Verdict: Evolution, Young Players and Backroom ImpactLiverpool head coach Andoni Iraola has had a straightforward assessment of the club’s pre-season work in the...
fullText:
Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola has had a straightforward assessment of the club’s pre-season work in the United States. So far, he likes what he has seen, and more importantly, he likes what it is starting to become.

There have been wins over Sunderland, 4-2, and Wrexham, 1-0, with one more fixture against Leeds United in Chicago to close the trip. Results in pre-season only matter up to a point. What matters more is whether the coach is getting through to the group, whether the group can absorb the ideas quickly, and whether the younger players can be trusted when the serious football starts.

On that front, Iraola’s verdict was clear. The USA camp has been, in his words, “really, really useful.” That is the key line because it gets to the point of pre-season. This is not about box-ticking, nor is it about pretending friendlies tell you everything. It is about time, repetition, habits and understanding.

As Iraola explained, “Obviously, you spend a lot of time with the players, with the staff, you get all the information you can.” That has value for a new head coach walking into a club that needs clarity, structure and a fresh football identity before the 2026-27 campaign begins.

Iraola used one word that matters more than any other at this stage, “evolution”. He said, “I think there is also an evolution, it has to be. We start to understand each other better, what we need to do. Every game, I hope we can get closer and closer and put ourselves in a position where the few players that still are not here start to train also, they are helped by the others.”

That is practical management talk. He is describing the early phase of installing a system. The shape, pressing triggers, distances between units and reactions in transition do not become automatic overnight. They need drilling, they need repetition and they need buy-in from players who understand what is being asked of them.

That is why this Liverpool USA tour matters. It gives Iraola long training days, meetings, recovery sessions and game situations. It also gives him a look at who processes information quickly and who still needs guidance. By the time the Premier League season opens, the expectation will be that Liverpool are already far sharper than they were at the start of this process.

If there has been one major positive from the trip, Iraola did not hesitate. “Probably the performance of the young players,” he said. That matters because managers often praise Academy talent in broad terms. Iraola went further and made it specific.

His judgment was that Liverpool’s youngsters “have performed really well against Premier League opposition, very good players – winning duels, helping us also in the collective idea.” That is the important bit. This is not praise based on enthusiasm or energy alone. He is talking about output in competitive moments, physical competitiveness and tactical discipline within the team structure.

He then added, “I think it probably has been the best, I wouldn’t say surprise but at least the confirmation.” Again, blunt and useful. He expected something, and what he has seen has confirmed the level is real.

That now leaves Liverpool with decisions to make. Some players will drop back to the U21s. Some will leave on loan. Some, according to Iraola, are already pushing for a genuine role in the senior squad. “They’ve shown me that they have the level, they can give us quality minutes, a good level in training and I’m sure some of them will stay with us, yes.”

There is no need to overcomplicate it. If a young player can help you in training, hold the level tactically and physically, and contribute proper minutes across a season, he stays in the picture. Liverpool have clearly had several do exactly that on this trip.

Iraola also made a point of highlighting the coaching staff around him, and he did so in practical terms. Shaun Cooper and Tommy Elphick are familiar faces from his previous work, and he values them because they understand both the game and the environment.

“Yes, for me, Tommy and Shaun are very valuable because they have been English players, they’ve played in the Premier League, the Championship, League One; they understand the culture, they understand what the players are thinking.” There is no mystery there. Coaches with dressing-room credibility and knowledge of the domestic game can save time for a head coach.

He also made clear why continuity matters. “They have seen all the process during these three years where we’ve been evolving, we’ve been adding different things.” That means they know the methods, the demands and the language of the coaching model. In a new environment, that matters.

Iraola was equally candid about the role assistants play behind the scenes. “I think they are sometimes in more touch with the players than me because always with the manager there is a little bit of more distance, I think the players are more comfortable sometimes with the assistants.” That is honest, and it is true in most dressing rooms. A good assistant does more than deliver drills. He reads mood, filters problems and keeps communication moving.

On Elphick’s personal connection to the club, Iraola offered a line that tells you plenty, “Tommy, I tell him, he is living his dream.” He added that Elphick had opportunities elsewhere but “he couldn’t miss this because he’s been a big Liverpool fan.”

There was also praise for new goalkeeping coach Alejandro Rosalen, whose appointment came through a club-led process. Iraola was direct about that too. “I didn’t know him personally, we’ve gone through a process led from the club, from the goalkeeping department, and we’ve decided he was the right guy.”

Rosalen arrives with a serious background, including years in Italy and top-level experience. Iraola pointed to that immediately, saying, “He has loads of experience, a lot of years at Fiorentina, a lot years in Napoli with some of the best coaches. He’s won the [Serie A title].”

Experience counts, but so does personality. Iraola stressed that side as well, “I’ve loved the personality once I could meet him and interview him. I liked a lot of the things. He brings good energy. I think he’s going to be a good help for our ’keepers. He’s doing really well, yes.”

That is where Liverpool stand after this phase of pre-season. Iraola sees progress. He sees young players who can contribute. He sees assistants who understand the job, and a goalkeeping coach who brings pedigree and energy. It is still July work for an August target, but there is a shape forming now. For Liverpool, that is the point of the tour, and for Iraola, it has already delivered something useful, a clearer picture of what his team can become.

title: Police in the US are making their own true crime podcasts
description: More police departments are trying to invigorate unsolved murder or missing cases through the power of podcasts.
fullText:
Peter Chadwick had been on the run for nearly four years, charged with murdering his wife, when California police launched a podcast about the crime.

He was captured in Mexico 10 months and 20 days later.

Karen Schepers had been missing for more than four decades when another police force, in Illinois, debuted the first episode of a podcast last year about the cold case - and her body was found at the bottom of a river within weeks.

Now Colorado investigators are hoping to bring in elusive tips about a 10-year-old unsolved murder, too. The Aurora Police Department (APD) released its own podcast this summer in an attempt to achieve justice for Chelsea Yasser, 21, who was found fatally stabbed in a shopping centre parking lot in 2016.

As the barrelling behemoth of true crime content continues to flourish, police departments across the US and abroad are turning to podcast production for help solving cold murder cases and other investigations.

"The true crime genre - whether it's TV, whether it's podcasts, whether it's books – I mean, it's wildly popular," says Joe Moylan, Aurora Police Department's public information officer. "And we absolutely were deliberate in trying to tap into that broader audience."

The phenomenon is still in its infancy and brings its own benefits and pitfalls - but experts believe the trend will grow.

"I think it's a tool that everyone will eventually embrace," says Michael Alcazar, retired NYPD detective and adjunct professor at John Jay College of Criminal Justice. True crime podcasts can air inaccurate information, he says, but this way police get to control what is out there and seek new tip-offs.

There were already plenty of podcasts featuring former detectives discussing cases or policing issues, says Alyce McGovern, associate professor in criminology at University of New South Wales in Australia, where law enforcement has also begun dipping its toes into podcast production.

But it's rarer for police department-produced podcasts to focus on cold cases and solicit tips, as the California, Colorado and Illinois departments have done.

The police programmes are episodic in nature, outlining the crimes, victims and investigations with narrative panache and interesting details - much the same way that groundbreaking true crime podcast Serial did when it debuted in 2014.

In Aurora, police hoped to produce a podcast that was equally engaging - and would prompt listeners to come forward with any relevant information.

The killing of Chelsea Yasser has been described by the podcasters as the "White Whale", of Moby Dick fame, given how long it has haunted investigators.

Yasser was fatally stabbed after getting into a minivan that pulled up in the parking lot; she collapsed moments after leaving the vehicle. Grainy surveillance footage captured the rocking van as the assault took place, but the images were not clear enough to discern a face and DNA recovered from under her fingernails matched no one in the system.

As the APD released the podcast in June, detectives were testing the DNA using new forensic genealogy technology, and the programme updated listeners about other new lines of enquiry.

The department has issued appeals for information on the Yasser murder before, but the podcast can cast a far wider net for witnesses and tipsters, Moylan says.

"If you weren't watching the news that night when it happened, or if you didn't pick up a newspaper, you might not know anything about this case, so we wanted to tap into that broader audience.

"Assuming that the suspect is still alive and out there somewhere, they could be anywhere in the country."

The podcast had been downloaded 7,184 times by the end of July, according to APD - yielding several tips, including one which investigators continue to pursue.

Most departments don't have the staff, budget or time needed to produce podcast content, nor do they have the equipment or expertise.

Others hold off for fear of repercussions, lawsuits and civil liability, says retired detective Alcazar.

In California, Newport Beach Police Department's podcast about the fugitive Chadwick, for example, was not without controversy. The millionaire was introduced to viewers in Episode 1 as "a man who killed his wife in the peaceful coastal community of Newport Beach, California in October 2012".

Chadwick had been charged and pleaded not guilty, but not tried - yet the podcast made no use of the word "alleged" and called the millionaire a "murderer". Critics argued that it flew in the face of innocent-before-proven-guilty parameters and that the job of police was to investigate, not adjudicate.

The podcast was produced and hosted by public information officer Jennifer Manzella, who defended the choice at the time, saying police "put out the same kinds of statements all the time".

She tells BBC News that she was trying to balance telling the story in an engaging way without jeopardising the investigation.

After Chadwick's August 2019 apprehension, he pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and was sentenced to 15 years to life in prison - where he remains.

Manzella says it wasn't a direct tip from the podcast that led to his capture - but it undeniably helped because it put pressure on Chadwick while on the run, making him more likely to make mistakes.

And investigators were able to obtain warrants and extraditions "in record time" because of the awareness - the podcast hit Number 24 on the iTunes chart.

In the wake of the podcast - and Chadwick's capture - she got calls from other departments and agencies interested in producing something similar.

But not everyone has been behind the idea.

"I initially was not really interested in it," says Detective Andrew Houghton - and now podcast co-host - at Elgin Police Department in Illinois. He worked on Elgin's 2025 podcast Somebody Knows Something alongside Detective Matthew Vartarian with assistance from a local radio station.

Houghton and Vartarian had just been assigned to Elgin's new cold case unit in 2024 when the chief informed them that the job would also involve podcasting.

"We're already starting this new unit," Houghton recalls. "Why are we adding something else new on top of that?"

Houghton and his partner begrudgingly began figuring out how to arrange episodes and soon discovered the process was also helping them structure the investigation. They formed different theories about what had happened to the missing 23-year-old, and each theory naturally formed an episode.

The podcast not only generated tips but also gave the detectives more ways to find leads. They started going through posts on social media about their own programme.

"They'd say, like, 'Oh, my mom worked with this person, or I live in this neighbourhood and I remember this.'"

The detectives ultimately solved the case through old-fashioned policework; one of their theories had been that Schepers had crashed her car and ended up in the river.

They had found a 1999 local newspaper story claiming that police had searched salvage yards by helicopter as well as dragging the Fox River but there was no evidence the latter had happened. And they did not shy away from telling listeners this.

So the department brought in a search company with the latest sonar technology as well as divers - and they found Schepers and her car at the bottom of the river in March 2025.

Now they're on the third season of the podcast. They shook up the format for the second, focusing on homicides, but have returned to a missing persons case.

Houghton acknowledges that "it is a lot of work - it takes a lot of time and effort".

As other departments navigate those budgetary and resource issues, however, there's a consensus that podcasts as an investigative tool will be seen more frequently.

If police departments can find the staffing to sustain it, podcasting could help in both recruitment and staff retention, says Janice Iwama, associate professor in American University's department of justice, law and criminology. It gives listeners the chance to learn more about what policing is really like, from the mouths of working officers.

Generational change could also fuel the trend, says retired NYPD Detective Alcazar, because younger police officers will be more ready to embrace the opportunities presented by podcasts and social media.

"That's their world," he says. "That's what they're most comfortable with."

title: An old-new take on argument parsing in Rust
description:
Extending getopts into a small framework for Unix-style Rust command-line tools.
Over the years, I’ve written tens of command-line applications in many different languages—shell is probably the top contender, believe it or not—and for various ecosystems. Along the way, I’ve developed… let’s say… opinions on how they should behave. But behavior and implementation are different topics, and today I would like to talk a little about the latter in the Rust ecosystem.
fullText:
Extending getopts into a small framework for Unix-style Rust command-line tools.

Over the years, I’ve written tens of command-line applications in many different languages—shell is probably the top contender, believe it or not—and for various ecosystems. Along the way, I’ve developed… let’s say… opinions on how they should behave. But behavior and implementation are different topics, and today I would like to talk a little about the latter in the Rust ecosystem.

A big theme behind those opinions is that consistency usually wins: when designing an application, you should target an ecosystem and make sure the tool feels “at home” within it instead of reinventing the way it accepts arguments or presents help.

For example: if you were to write a command-line application in Go, you’d naturally reach for the built-in flag library to define flags. Doing so would make the tool feel normal to other Go developers and would make it easier to “read” to them—but the end user does not care, dare I say… at all, which language your tool is written in. So if they try to use such a tool in the context of standard Unix tools like those provided by coreutils or textutils, your tool will feel out of place. And that is what matters to me: I develop tools for a certain ecosystem, not for a language, and I want those tools to integrate well no matter which language they are written in.

I mentioned Go right above because Go is the prime example of opinionated choices that “leak” in various ways. This article is about Rust, however, so let’s switch languages.

When writing Rust command-line applications, the expectation nowadays—or rather, assumption—is that you’ll use the clap crate to parse options and arguments. Funnily enough, this assumption is so ingrained in the ecosystem that, when I asked a late-2025 coding agent to review a codebase of mine, it hallucinated that I was using clap even when such crate was nowhere to be found.

Here is what a simple clap-based hello world app looks like:

I will not deny that the resulting app looks nice and that the declarative idiom to define this interface is concise and very powerful. But the result is… out of place with other programs because of all these colors (I know they can be disabled). Also, the code is a bit too magical, as usually happens with #[derive]-style libraries (I know you can opt out of that).

And yet… even with all the bells and whistles, the library doesn’t provide enough mechanisms to define an app “end to end”. You see: Rust’s main can return an ExitCode, which is enough to report success or failure to the caller, but this still leaves the application’s control flow in your hands. Because you have to explicitly call clap within main, there is no guarantee that you do it at “the right time”: you might be tempted to parse config files before parsing arguments and other nasty things like that, which can then lead to weird behavior like --help not working if the config file is malformed or on an unavailable network drive.

clap isn’t the only game in town though. There are indeed other Rust libraries to parse command lines, with argh being another popular choice. Some of these are also built around derives, some make different tradeoffs around help text and output style, and some smaller alternatives focus mostly on parsing options. This is all fine, but it still doesn’t give me the small Unix-y framework I wanted: something that treats options and positional arguments as one interface, validates both consistently, and owns the startup sequence from parsing to exit code.

For all of the reasons above, I’ve developed “my own ways” to parse options and arguments in Rust so that they align with more traditional Unix-y programs. In doing so, I ended up writing my own library. I initially wrote this library in the context of the EndBOX where I had to implement various system services and wanted:

I called that library libapp at the time and, in the fall of 2025, I thought of cleaning it up a little and publishing it. So, today, I want to belatedly announce getoptsargs. Mind you, I had drafted this article back in November but never published it, so today is the day. Better late than never.

You might be thinking that getoptsargs is quite a mouthful, and even an ugly name. And you know what? That’s true. But the name is what it is because getoptsargs builds on and extends the ancient getopts, in the tradition of Unix-like systems. getopts is largely unused today in the Rust ecosystem—except for the tiny little fact that rustc itself uses it.

OK, OK, if you want me to be perfectly honest… the reason getoptsargs exists at all is because getopts is what I originally picked up in 2016 when I started learning Rust based on my previous knowledge of the POSIX getopt and the GNU getopts libc functions… and I never switched gears.

getoptsargs is basically a wrapper over getopts, extending it to offer argument-parsing facilities. Where getopts leaves you with a list of free-form strings to validate by hand, getoptsargs lets you:

As such, its API tries to follow the same interfaces that getopts offers, which means I’ve kept original names intact and modeled my own extensions in a similar fashion. This leads to rather cryptic method names and suboptimal Rust interfaces, but again, I tried to mimic getopts as much as possible.

What I’ve changed, however, is the way in which you should use the library. getoptsargs provides an “end-to-end” framework to define the main method of an application, and it does so with three pieces. The first is the application Builder, which is a struct that implements the builder pattern to register application metadata, options, and arguments. The second is the command-line Matches, which extends the getopts struct for parsed options with access to parsed arguments. And the third is an app macro that facilitates writing the scaffolding for main, delegating to a couple of functions.

A sample, full-featured getoptsargs program looks like this:

And then we can run it in various ways:

You might still say: there is too much magic in those macros and builders! And you’re right, so you can also define the same app using imperative code and avoid all of that. To see how, I’ll refer you to the various upstream examples.

I do not intend for this crate to replace the nicer clap or argh or the other libraries that exist out there. Heck, I do not even expect any of you to want to use it. But I still have a use for something like this in my own programs, and I wanted to factor out the code I had already written into a cohesive standalone piece, so I had to publish the crate.

Head to https://github.com/jmmv/getoptsargs/

title: Tone Generator
description: Free online tone generator. Play any frequency from 1 Hz to 20 kHz with sine, square, saw or triangle waves. Test speakers, tune, check your hearing.
fullText:
A tone generator plays one clean sound at the pitch you choose. You type a number in hertz (Hz) and the tool plays that exact tone. It all happens inside your browser, so the sound starts the moment you press play. Nothing to download, nothing to set up.

You can play a low 40 Hz tone that you feel more than hear, a middle tone like 440 Hz, or a 15,000 Hz tone near the top of human hearing. Some people call this an hz generator; others call it a frequency generator. Same thing.

Play anything from 1 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Type a number, or step it one hertz at a time.

Sine is the cleanest tone. Square, sawtooth and triangle sound fuller and sharper.

Send the sound to one side or keep it centred, so you can test each speaker on its own.

Move a slider and the sound follows while it plays. No stopping and starting.

Copy a link that remembers your tone. Anyone who opens it hears the same thing.

Phone, tablet or computer — the tool behaves the same on all of them.

Start with what you're trying to hear. Around 20 to 60 Hz is where subwoofers live, so that range shows up rattles in a car door or a loose speaker grille. The middle of the range, roughly 200 Hz to 2 kHz, is where voices sit, and it's the easiest place to judge whether two speakers are matched. Above 10 kHz you're testing tweeters and your own ears at the same time.

For tuning, 440 Hz is the standard A that most orchestras and apps use. Use the sine shape for anything you want to match by ear — the other shapes add extra tones on top and make pitch harder to judge.

A sine wave is a single frequency and nothing else. It sounds smooth, almost hollow, and it's the right choice for testing and tuning.

Square, sawtooth and triangle waves stack extra frequencies on top of the one you picked. That's why they sound brighter or buzzier at the same number of hertz. Square waves are handy for hearing whether a speaker distorts; sawtooth is closer to a synth or a string sound; triangle sits in between and is gentler on the ears than square.

title: A deep dive into Nvidia's Vera CPU and the Olympus cores that power it
description: 88 custom cores, 176 funky threads, 1.5 TB of laptop RAM, and 1.8 TB/s of NVLink connectivity — this isn't your typical datacenter chip
fullText:
88 custom cores, 176 funky threads, 1.5 TB of laptop RAM, and 1.8 TB/s of NVLink connectivity — this isn't your typical datacenter chip

DEEP DIVE For the first time, Nvidia has directly challenged Intel and AMD's CPU dominance. With the launch of Vera, the AI arms dealer aims to flog its standalone CPUs to as many hyperscalers and other cloud providers as it can.

Alibaba, ByteDance, Meta, Oracle, CoreWeave, Lambda, Nebius, and NScale have already signed up to deploy the chips in their respective clouds.

The follow-on to Nvidia's Grace CPU promises 88 custom Armv9.2 cores, 176 threads, support for up to 1.5 TB of LPDDR5X memory, and, critically, availability as a standalone platform independent of Nvidia's GPUs.

But beyond that, and a mountain of marketing about how it'll be the best CPU for everything AI, Vera's inner workings have largely remained a mystery until recently.

That changed late last month, when Nvidia released a whitepaper spilling the beans on its first fully-custom CPU, which is far weirder than anyone could have anticipated.

Ostensibly, Nvidia is aiming Vera at two key workloads: the first and least surprising is as the AI head node responsible for managing the GPUs in its upcoming Vera Rubin systems. The second, and more contentious, is as a host for AI agents, which, unlike the large language models (LLMs) that power them, don't actually run on GPUs.

From what we gather, much of Vera's core architecture is predicated on quashing pipeline and execution bottlenecks in order to make it more effective in these roles. But before we dive into Nvidia's Olympus core, let's revisit the chip itself.

Peel back Vera's rather substantial heat spreader and you'll find an assortment of chiplets responsible for I/O, memory, and compute. However, this isn't another rehash of the chiplet architecture popularized by AMD.

Unlike x86 processor makers, which spread dozens of cores across multiple dies, Vera's compute die is monolithic. All 88 cores are housed in one big chunk of silicon that from what we understand is fabbed on TSMC's 3nm process. Nvidia argues its monolithic compute architecture has benefits for both core-to-core bandwidth and latency compared to competing designs.

Surrounding the compute die is an assortment of chiplets, including eight LPDDR5x controllers, and what appears to be two distinct I/O dies, one responsible for PCIe 6.4 and CXL 3.1 connectivity and another dedicated to the chip's NVLink Chip-to-Chip interface.

In terms of package design, Vera is somewhat reminiscent of Amazon's Graviton 4 CPUs, which also combine a monolithic compute die while disaggregating the I/O and memory functionality to dedicated silicon.

Like most modern datacenter CPUs, Vera supports both single- and dual-socket configurations, the latter of which Nvidia calls the Vera CPU Superchip.

Unveiled at GTC in March, the Superchip features two Vera CPUs connected over NVLink-C2C at a blisteringly fast 1.8 TB/s of bidirectional bandwidth, for a total of 176 cores and 352 threads.

The two chips are fed by 16 SOCAMM2 LPDDR5x memory modules, which deliver 2.4 TB/s of aggregate memory bandwidth (1.2 TB/s each) — roughly twice the bandwidth of AMD's Turin Epycs, which were launched in 2024.

Nvidia's agentic AI reference designs call for cramming as many as 128 of these superchips (256 CPUs) totaling 22,528 cores and 384 TB of memory into a single liquid-cooled rack.

Previously, Nvidia had relied on off-the-shelf CPU cores from Arm. For example, depending on the iteration, Nvidia's Grace CPUs used Arm's Neoverse V2 (GB200/300), Neoverse V3 (AGX Thor), or Cortex X925 and A725 cores (GB10), depending on which was most convenient.

With Vera, Nvidia has moved on to designing its own ARMv9.2-compatible core, called Olympus. In fact, it's up for debate how custom the chip really is. We've been told that the chip builds heavily on existing Arm IP, and looking at Olympus' architectural block diagram, we can see why.

Olympus features a 10-wide decoder and dispatch, eight integer arithmetic logic units (ALUs), six vector/FP pipelines (SVE 128), four load units, and 2x store units. So it's got a fat front and back end compared to the Zen 5 cores found in AMD's Turin Epycs or the Redwood Cove cores used by Intel's Granite Rapids Xeons.

But compared to off-the-shelf Arm cores, Olympus' front and back end aren't breaking any records. In fact, Olympus looks a lot like a heavily modified Cortex X925.

With that said, Nvidia claims Olympus features an entirely custom neural branch predictor, which is capable of exploring two branches simultaneously.

Branch prediction is key to performance in modern CPUs, and involves anticipating future code paths and executing down them before they're needed. By predicting two paths per cycle, Vera decreases the likelihood of a mispredict, theoretically boosting its performance in the process.

And from what we can tell, a lot of the customization that went into Vera was made explicitly to stamp out pipeline and execution bubbles in order to maximize the number of instructions per clock (IPC).

In particular, Nvidia claims its neural branch predictor delivers higher hit rates than history-based approaches, making it ideal for running branch-heavy workloads, like the Python scripts generated on the fly by AI code assistants.

Nvidia also claims to have made several innovations to the mid-core, again aimed at mitigating pipeline stalls. Memory renaming speeds up store-to-load dependency chains by allowing dependent instructions to execute before a load completes if the relationship to the data can be divined.

"This is particularly beneficial for pointer-heavy software, graph traversal, runtime frameworks, and complex object-oriented workloads," the company explained.

Nvidia also implemented a value prediction scheme which "identifies stable dependency chains and predicts future values before they are produced, allowing dependent instructions to execute speculatively while correctness is verified later."

This functionality, the company claims, helps to speed up repetitive software patterns and sequential data processing.

On the back end, Nvidia Olympus features a similar complement of ALUs and FP units as the X925, but they've been implemented differently. Eight of the ALUs are simple integer units which handle basic mathematics, while the company says two complex ALUs handle multiplication and division, CRC, and shift intensive workloads.

The back end also features four dedicated branch units that work with the chip's branch predictor to resolve control flow decisions that would otherwise cause pipeline stalls.

Meanwhile, for floating point operations, Olympus features six 128-bit Arm scalable vector engines (SVE2) extensions which also support FP8, along with a pair of vector units dedicated to speeding up crypto operations.

Each core is supported by a 64 KB L1 instruction cache, 96 KB L1 data cache, and 2MB per core of L2. The chip also features 164 MB of system level cache (SLC) that's sharded across the chip.

Perhaps Olympus' most interesting party trick is support for simultaneous multithreading (SMT).

SMT has been a mainstay of x86 chips since 2002. The technology boosts utilization by enabling two threads to harness idle execution units during a single cycle. While SMT doesn’t double throughput, for certain applications it can deliver double-digit percentage gains.

While Arm has supported SMT in the past — you may recall Cavium ThunderX2's four-way SMT implementation prior to its acquisition by Marvell — the company has downplayed its value with its own agentic CPU.

Arm's dislike for the tech didn't stop Nvidia from implementing SMT-like functionality in Olympus. We say SMT-like because it's not SMT in the conventional sense. Rather than simultaneous multi-threading, Nvidia markets it as spatial multithreading, which is an apt name given how it works.

Rather than two threads that share the resources of one core, Olympus' SMT implementation looks more like core bifurcation with a shared cache line. You can either have one fat core or two skinny ones. To our eyes, it looks a bit like multi-instance GPU (MIG) for the CPU.

The white paper makes a big to-do about how spatial multithreading avoids the thread contention you can see with x86 parts, which makes sense, because Nvidia's threads behave more like individual cores. We wouldn't read too much into these claims, though. There have always been applications that benefit from SMT and those that don't, and it's easy enough to turn it off if you don't want it.

With that, Nvidia's SMT implementation could be beneficial to agent sandboxes for agentic workloads. With containers — that's all these sandboxes really are – there are two workloads. There's the job you're running inside the container – let's say a Python script and interpreter  – and then there's the container runtime, which is responsible for orchestration of container workloads and managing networking and storage overlays.

These are very different jobs. By bifurcating its cores, Nvidia can keep the workload and runtime separate, which in theory should make for more deterministic performance.

Before we move on to Vera's memory subsystem, we need to spend a few minutes discussing Nvidia's second-gen scalable coherency fabric (SCF), which is used to stitch all 88 cores together.

As we mentioned earlier, Vera features a monolithic compute die, which means all of its cores are packed on the same silicon. The SCF is essentially a cache-coherent superhighway designed to connect cores together at a whopping 3.4 TB/s of bisectional bandwidth.

As Nvidia explains it: "SCF is organized as a distributed coherent interconnect connecting multiple cores through a collection of Coherency Switch Nodes (CSNs). Each CSN connects up to two cores and serves as a routing point within the fabric, enabling efficient movement of requests between cores, caches, memory controllers, and external interfaces."

The SCF is also where the L3 cache lives, which explains why Nvidia opted to shard its SLC across the CPU rather than having one big, centrally located pool of it.

The SCF is critical, as without it, Vera wouldn't actually be able to utilize its memory bandwidth effectively.

Vera features eight LPDDR5x memory controllers with support for SOCAMM2 modules up to 9600 MT/s. At 1.2 TB/s and roughly 14 GB/s per core, Vera has one of the fastest memory subsystems in the world today, but it's worth pointing out that the competition's chips launched nearly two years ago.

Both Intel and AMD's next-gen CPUs will make the jump to 16 memory channels. We're still waiting on details on Intel's 192-core Diamond Rapids platform, but we learned last week that AMD's Venice CPUs will boast up to 256 cores and support for 8,000 MT/s RDIMMs or 12,800 MT/s MRDIMMs, which translates to between 1 TB/s and 1.6 TB/s.

Assuming AMD's GMI-links aren't a bottleneck this time around, the House of Zen's 96-core Epycs should hit around 17 GB/s per core, and there's no reason to think Intel's Xeon 7 processors won't do the same.

With that said, Vera's memory subsystem should suck a bit less power thanks to the use of LPDDR5X rather than standard RDIMMs. The company claims under a sustained load, its memory subsystem contributes just 30 to 40 watts of consumption versus 100 to 200 watts depending on channel and DIMM count on a traditional server platform. For reference, Vera's TDP is configurable between 250W and 450W.

Power consumption might explain why AMD is working on a new Epyc, codenamed Verano, which will also use LPDDR5X.

Vera isn't bursting just with memory bandwidth, but with I/O bandwidth as well. The chip is among the first to support PCIe 6.4 and CXL 3.1, beating out Intel, and possibly AMD depending on the first systems to actually make it into customers' hands.

As with past generational PCIe bumps, 6.0 sees per lane bandwidth double to 64 Gbps, which translates to 128 GB/s (256 GB/s bidirectional) for a single x16 slot. A single Vera socket can support 6 such slots (96 lanes in total) for connectivity to NICs, storage, and other peripherals. In the dual-socket Vera CPU superchip config, the lane count does drop slightly to 176 lanes or 11 x16 slots.

Along with PCIe, those lanes also support Compute Express Link 3.1. CXL has been around for a while now, but the 3.1 iteration is notable for its support for fabrics and memory sharing.

As we've previously discussed, this capability opens the door to network attached memory appliances — which we affectionately call memory godboxes — where multiple CPUs can share the memory.

Finally, we need to talk a bit about Vera's NVLink chip-to-chip connectivity. First introduced back in its Grace CPUs, the high-speed interconnect's bandwidth has now been doubled to 1.8 TB/s of bidirectional bandwidth (900 GB/s up and down).

This high-speed interconnect allows for coherent memory access across connected CPUs or GPUs. In the Vera Rubin superchip, NVLink is how the CPU talks to the two GPUs. Meanwhile for Vera CPU superchip, the NVLink-C2C interface provides a blazing fast interconnect that mitigates many of the bandwidth bottlenecks associated with multi-socket systems.

In agentic workloads, Nvidia estimates Vera will deliver 1.8x higher per-core performance than AMD's 128-core Epyc 9755 in benchmarks representative of agentic workloads, and up to 2.6x faster performance in graph traversal jobs.

While that sounds impressive, we're not reading too deeply into Nvidia's performance claims just yet. Turin launched nearly two years ago, which makes it an advantageous comparison point. CPU benchmarks are notoriously easy to cherry pick, and microbenchmarks, while useful for quantifying hardware's capabilities, aren't always representative of real-world performance.

A classic example of this is core-to-core latency on early AMD Epycs versus Intel Xeons. As we've already established, AMD employs a multi-chiplet architecture that, for Turin, used up to eight frequency-optimized cores or 16 density-optimized cores per core-complex die (CCD).

For workloads that can fit within a single CCD, the core-to-core latency is extremely small. But if a core on one CCD needs to talk to a core on another CCD, it has to walk the I/O die, which incurs a stiff performance penalty.

Intel, until recently, has favored higher core-count compute dies, which historically have fared better for latency-sensitive applications, like databases, for the same reason Nvidia opted for a big monolithic compute die on Vera.

Whether this actually confers an advantage varies from application to application, and it's not a clear cut victory for one approach or the other. Both have their merits. AMD's chiplet architecture lets them use smaller, better yielding dies, which translates to better margins.

We should also mention that Venice makes the jump to 12- and 32-core CCDs, which means the workload would need to be even more talkative for you to notice the latency hit.

We've said it before and we'll say it again: there has never been and never will be one CPU to rule them all. Vera doesn't change that.

After getting a peek at Vera's performance in the Phoronix Test Suite in a selected, Nvidia-dictated set of tests earlier this year, we're optimistic about Vera's performance in its target workloads, but look forward to seeing fully independent runs on production hardware, especially with AMD's Venice just a few months away.

We fully anticipate Vera to sell extremely well, if not for its performance characteristics, then because if you want more than eight Rubins, it's probably coming with a Vera CPU attached. ®

title: Mathematics Without Mathematicians
description: We must know. We shall not know.
fullText:
Yesterday, OpenAI announced the solution to ten open problems in
mathematics, all discovered by a yet-unreleased model. There’s only one, the
coding theory one, where I know enough to say “huh, that’s important”, but
according to the mathematicians I trust this is important.

Inevitably, people will spin some sophistry to cope, to convince themselves
nothing will change. And that’s fine. People need to cope. But we can’t put our
heads in the sand forever while the world is transformed around us. So, here is
a list of ways people will cope about AI taking over mathematics, and how each
cope is likely to be refuted by reality.

My intent is not to horribly depress everyone but rather to help them metabolize
the implications of this technology. The arguments here are somewhat portable:
replace “mathematics” with “botany” or whatever as needed.

Obvious and not worth addressing.

“We will direct the AIs, point them at problems and research areas
to solve.”

The AIs will exceed humans in taste and intuition. At some point, the
human pointing the way will get worse results than the human saying “here’s a
proof checker, have fun” and paying for the tokens.

“We will teach the mathematics AI discovers.”

The AIs will be better teachers than the humans. In any case, there won’t be a
human audience for expository work of frontier math.

“We will choose how to canonize the results AI discovers.”

This is a nice cope. The AIs are explorers out in the frontiers, the humans
gratefully receive their Lean proofs, and then discourse over them, choose which
results are relevant, shape those results into a little brick for the great
cathedral of algebra. Analogous to the above: the AIs will build the
cathedral on their own. They will be better architects than us.

“We will become students of AI mathematics.”

This works until the AIs have blasted so deep into the deductive closure of
mathlib that the distance from elementary mathematics to the frontier exceeds
what any human can hope to learn in their lifetime, no matter how narrow their
focus.

“We need humans to understand the results AI discovers.”

We won’t! This misunderstands who the audience will be. AIs will do frontier
math, downstream, AIs will use the new math to do frontier science, finally, AIs
will use the new science to do frontier engineering. No human needs to
understand any of it, firms that put humans in the loop to understand the
results will be outcompeted by those which don’t.

The result is that we will live in a demon-haunted world, full of marvelous
devices whose operation we will not understand, based on engineering principles
we will not understand, discovered using formalisms we will not understand.

“Computers are already superhuman at chess, yet we still play chess.”

Unlike most copes, I think this one is interesting. Computers are superhuman
chess players, yet we don’t care, and continue playing as normal. Why should
mathematics be different?

The main reason, I think, is that chess is self-contained: results from chess
don’t help us understand the orbits of the planets or the binding of drugs to
protein surfaces. But mathematics, famously, is the great dynamo of
science, the best language and method for understanding the world. A machine
that can replace a human mathematician, but better and faster and cheaper, is
materially useful; a better chess engine is not.

If two computers which are superhuman at chess play against each other, who
cares? There is little demand for this, so there is no-one to outcompete. A
superhuman mathematician is different.

“Mathematics will change, but mathematicians and the mathematically-inclined
will still do math on their own.”

I think this ignores that mathematics is embedded in a social context. As an
example: when it became clear that AI would eat software, my cope was: “I’m
perfectly happy to become an engineering manager to agents in my professional
life; in my off time, I can still write code for the pleasure of it.”

And I do. But this cope ignores the effect AI has had on the social context of
writing code: the discourse has gotten worse, and vastly more anti-intellectual;
people who used to talk about type systems and compilers now talk about “loops”
and “harnesses”; you put a hand-created project on GitHub and you get slop PRs;
you open a link to an interesting-looking project and find the README is
unreadable AI slop. And in the long-term, it is demoralizing to ponder: will
anyone design a new programming language? Dually, if I design a new language,
will anyone care? If I write a library that introduces an elegant new formalism
to solve a particular problem, will anyone use it?

Which is to say: no man is an island. You can do mathematics on your own, but
you’ll find that very, very few people can sustain any activity long-term on the
basis of intrinsic motivation alone. We are social animals: we care about being
useful, about status, about outcomes in the world.

I think I should end on a cheerful note. So let me try. Personally, I don’t
believe technology is inevitable. “Inevitable” is a word reserved for the orbits
of the planets. Nothing that is the product of human action is inevitable. We
can choose to obsolete ourselves, and we can choose not to. We can realize that
AGI is a devil’s bargain: we may accelerate technical progress, we may
unlock all kinds of wonderful tech tree nodes like life extension earlier than
we would otherwise; but the result, in the long run, is that humans become, at
best, like pets under the care of vastly more powerful entities.

The future is not certain, but I’ve phrased everything above as definitive for
simplicity. If we take the possibility of AGI and ASI seriously, if AI continues
to progress as it has for the past ~6 years, I think this is a reasonable view
of where things will go.

Probably the best argument against AI progress is “RL doesn’t generalize well,
we have seen immense progress in verifiable domains like formalized mathematics
and coding, we will see less progress in domains that are intuitive or
unformalizable”. Maybe true. But billions of dollars and thousands of very smart
people—and, increasingly, very smart models—are being thrown at this
problem. How long does this cope last?

title: I built a personal CRM that lives inside Apple's Contacts app
Aevros .... A kernel that explains itself
description: A self-explaining operating system that turns kernel internals into answers - Mobeen0119/Aevros
fullText:
An operating system that explains itself.

Philosophy • Architecture • Shell Commands • Building • Contributing

Aevros is a small operating system kernel, written from scratch in C and x86 assembly.

It exists to answer a question most educational kernels don't bother with: not just what broke, but why. "Something went wrong" has never been useful information to anyone, ever.

Everything was written from scratch so every subsystem can be understood and modified without hidden dependencies.

The part that makes it different: a handful of built-in tools let the system explain its own state, in plain English, from inside the shell instead of hex dump. Kill a process and see exactly what you just ruined. Inspect an allocation and find out who's responsible for it. Trigger a page fault and get a sentence back instead of a wall of hex doing its best to ruin your afternoon.

That's the whole project in one line: a kernel that can answer "why" about itself. Full writeup in docs/PHILOSOPHY.md.

This is health, one of the introspection tools, reporting on the system live:

And this is fork() and exec() actually running, a process forking into a parent and a child, then loading and running an ELF binary:

No debugger. No print statements added for the screenshot. The kernel just answers the question, this is what that looks like.

Few Moments , and you're at a shell that can explain itself. Details: docs/BUILDING.md.

Every "Working" row has a real self-test in kernel/selftest.c, run selftest yourself. Full table: README implementation matrix in the repo.

Today, Aevros is a hobby kernel.

Long-term vision: it's the operating system you reach for when you're tired of guessing why something broke.

Because debugging should feel less like archaeology, and more like asking a question.

Aevros is under active development. Subsystems get rewritten as understanding improves, they don't get left alone just because they work. If you're evaluating this for anything beyond learning and experimentation, don't, not yet. That's not false modesty, it's just accurate: no full ring 3 isolation, no preemptive scheduler.

MIT, see LICENSE. Use it, modify it, ship it, including commercially, just keep the license and copyright notice attached.

Contributions welcome. Read CONTRIBUTING.md first, then docs/ARCHITECTURE.md to get oriented before touching a subsystem. Issues tagged good-first-issue are a decent place to start.
