title: How to search documents we can't read – Confer Blog
description: How Confer makes encrypted PDFs, Word documents, spreadsheets, and other folder files searchable without creating a plaintext document library.
fullText:
Confer now has folder files! You can add PDFs, Word documents, presentations, spreadsheets, HTML, Markdown, or plain text to a folder, and those files become available to every conversation inside it. Add something once, then ask about it whenever it becomes relevant.

An attachment stays with one conversation. A folder file is there for every conversation you start in that folder.

Imagine a folder called Health. It might contain lab reports, visit summaries, imaging reports, insurance explanations of benefits, and a medication list. Before seeing a new specialist, you could ask for a single timeline of diagnoses, medications, procedures, and unusual results, with each item linked back to its source. You could ask how a lab value has moved over five years, whether it changed after a medication was introduced, or where a symptom first appeared in your record.

Or imagine a Finances folder with tax returns, bank statements, benefits documents, a lease, and mortgage paperwork. You could ask why your mortgage payment went up, which subscriptions and insurance premiums have quietly increased, or where to find every number your accountant requested. You could trace an unfamiliar merchant across years of statements without opening a few dozen PDFs yourself.

The same idea works for a house (inspection report, contractor quotes, manuals, warranties), or a long-running project (papers, books, specifications, notes, spreadsheets). Rather than repeatedly attaching the same files to unrelated conversations, the folder becomes a persistent body of context that each conversation can draw from.

The feature itself is simple: instead of handing the assistant one document at a time, give it a filing cabinet. The catch is that filing cabinets tend to contain exactly what people are least comfortable giving an AI company – medical histories, bank statements, tax returns, contracts – and a collection of these documents is often more revealing than any one of them.

An LLM cannot read a PDF or Word document directly. Those files are binary containers full of encoded text, fonts, images, drawing instructions, page geometry, and other machinery. A multi-modal model can process raw text or images, so before it can do anything useful with a document, the file has to be translated into those forms.

Conventional non-private AI services begin by receiving the original file in plaintext and extracting the text embedded in it. Scanned pages require an additional OCR path (which isn’t supported by default for most services), or pages are rendered as images so the model can see things text extraction does not represent well, like tables, charts, forms, handwriting, and spatial layout.

The extracted text is then divided into smaller passages and indexed so that relevant sections can be found later without putting the entire document into the model’s context every time. By the time the document is ready to use, the service has several representations of it: the original file, extracted text, a search index, and – when visual processing is enabled – layout metadata and page images. All of the representations it creates are plaintext.

This makes retrieval easier, but it also gives the company operating the service a readable document library specifically organized to make the information inside it easy to find.

For Confer, we wanted the same useful result with a different privacy boundary. The original is encrypted before it leaves your device. It is decrypted only inside an attested Trusted Execution Environment (TEE), where the model also runs. Text extraction, indexing, retrieval, and inference all happen inside that boundary. The derivatives are encrypted before they leave the TEE, and are only opened there again when a later request needs them.

The document pipeline still works; it just never produces a durable plaintext copy that we can read.

Every folder file is encrypted on your device with a fresh, random 256-bit key before it is uploaded. Object storage receives ciphertext. The filename, key, and references required to use the file are kept in the folder’s encrypted metadata, protected by the same passkey-derived key hierarchy as the rest of Confer.

To prepare the document for search, the client sends its key and opaque storage reference through Confer’s attested encrypted channel into the TEE. The host machine cannot read the channel or inspect the TEE’s memory.

Inside that environment, the document is decrypted and transformed:

The resulting storage layout contains the original, the extracted text, and the search artifact – but all three are ciphertext protected by the file’s key. We get a durable search index without getting a document database that we can read.

When you start a conversation in the folder, your client decrypts the folder manifest locally. The file capabilities required for that request – an opaque object reference and its key – travel to the TEE over the encrypted inference channel.

These capabilities are orchestration state, not model arguments. The model never gets to choose a storage path or request an encryption key. It gets four fairly ordinary tools instead:

If you ask, “How has my A1C changed over the last three years?” the model can search the Health folder, read the pages surrounding matching lab results, and view a page when a table was not represented reliably in extracted text. Search terms and results are plaintext only inside the TEE. If a rendered page has to make a short trip through object storage, it is encrypted with a fresh key and given short-lived retention.

The model is running inside that same TEE, so retrieved text and rendered pages do not have to cross the privacy boundary to reach it.

This is basically retrieval-augmented generation, except the provider does not have a readable retrieval database.

The useful way to think about a TEE is as a place where sensitive computation happens, not as a permanent home for sensitive data. Confer’s TEE is stateless with respect to documents: during extraction it opens one source, produces encrypted derivatives, and discards the plaintext working state; during a question it opens the encrypted artifact, passes relevant evidence directly to the model running in the same TEE, and discards it again.

All durable document state outside the TEE is ciphertext, and keys arrive inside only when there is work to perform. This is what “stateless” means here: not that the files are forgotten, but that no plaintext document library or search database persists between requests.

Remote attestation makes this boundary verifiable. The client checks the code running inside the TEE against Confer’s reproducible build before sending any requests.

The result of all this is fairly mundane. Add files to a folder, and then start asking questions.

We think privacy technology is most successful when the result looks like an ordinary feature. Nobody wants an encrypted document extraction pipeline. They want a Health folder that helps them with insights, or a Finances folder that can find the number buried on page 47, without creating yet another company that knows the contents of both.

Don't have Confer? Give it a try!

title: Laura Loomer says Russian propaganda has influenced parts of the GOP
description: Loomer added the issue has been amplified by "the amount of brainwashing that is taking place on social media platforms."
fullText:
(NewsNation) — Conservative activist Laura Loomer believes parts of the GOP have been influenced by Russian and other foreign propaganda.

Loomer's remarks come after a recent trip to Ukraine, where she said seeing the effects of the war firsthand changed her views on the conflict. She said her perspective shifted after experiencing an air raid and hearing warning sirens.

Loomer also interviewed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and said the experience gave her a new understanding of the war and what she now considers Russian propaganda that had influenced some of her previous beliefs.

"I really have come to understand that everything that I was led to believe while living in this echo chamber, a very toxic echo chamber, that is supported by foreign governments," she told "Batya!"

Loomer said the problem has been amplified by what she described as "the amount of brainwashing that is taking place on social media platforms."

"American social media companies refuse to comply with sanctions law and they refuse to limit the tweets and the correspondences and the broadcasting of these entities that have been sanctioned," Loomer said.

While in Ukraine, Loomer said she spoke twice with President Donald Trump and shared details of her interview with Zelenskyy. She said she had also spent more than a year warning Trump and White House officials about individuals she believes are spreading foreign-backed messaging.

"I've prepared several very detailed reports on some of these personalities and the propaganda and the anti-Trump rhetoric that they have been pushing out to their audiences," she said.

"And unfortunately, because of their foreign propaganda and their incessant Trump hatred and their obsession with blaming Jews and blaming all of the world's issues on Donald Trump and Israel, so many people have been radicalized in the GOP. And so I've really made it a point to stress this to the White House," Loomer said.

Loomer said she was encouraged that Trump has publicly criticized figures including Tucker Carlson, Megyn Kelly and Candace Owens.

"I don't want to take credit for anything that Donald Trump has done because he's his own individual, and he thinks for himself, and he makes his own decisions," she said. "Despite preparing a lot of these reports for the White House, it's my understanding a lot of this information was not given to him or explained to him in full, which is alarming."

Loomer said Trump should take a harder line against individuals she believes are promoting foreign propaganda by enforcing stricter standards within his administration and political circle.

"I think his biggest political liability and the biggest detriment to social cohesion within the MAGA movement and cohesion within the GOP as we head into these perilous midterm elections is making sure that you don't have this albatross around the party's neck," Loomer said.

title: Despite China’s 996 culture, DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng says his workers don’t do overtime or even have KPIs: ‘No one manages them’
description: While Silicon Valley races to adopt China's brutal 996 culture, DeepSeek's founder says his $60 billion AI company has no KPIs and no overtime.
fullText:
In just three years, DeepSeek has gone from an unknown startup to a $60 billion AI powerhouse. The ChatGPT rival has had around 173 million downloads since it launched to the public in January 2025. And its founder Liang Wenfeng says he did it all without a single KPI or late-night shifts from his team.

"We generally don't work overtime," Liang revealed in a nearly four-hour discussion session with staff, obtained and transcribed by Tencent Technology.

And the world's richest AI founder explained that there are two reasons for his laid-back approach: "First, research needs a relaxed environment; if you push too hard, you can't do research. Second, we're very focused, which means we do very few things."

It's not just the working hours that are relaxed at DeepSeek. There's apparently no rigid hierarchy handing down orders, no rulebook employees are expected to follow, and no strict written end goal that workers need to adhere to daily. Even how they manage half of their working days is up to them.

"We don't really have an organization—we're driven by a vision, organized by a vision," Liang, who has a $37.9 billion net worth, added. "That vision isn't even written down. We've never written anything."

Employees aren't even given monthly targets to hit, and Wenfeng maintains that he's led by their consensus. "No one manages them. No KPIs," he said, before adding that they're only told what to do for half of their workday. "We hope 'formal work' doesn't take more than half of an employee's time. The other half is unallocated. They can do whatever they want."

It's a strikingly loose setup for a company sitting at the center of China's AI ambitions—not least because the country has a famously tough working culture.

China's 996 work schedule—that is, working 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. six days a week—was outlawed in 2021. But instead of going away, it's become a badge of honor among tech founders.

The habit runs deep in Chinese tech. E-commerce giant Alibaba, social media titan Tencent, and Alibaba rival JD.com have all leaned on 996 as part of their success story, often crediting their rise, in part, to the long hours logged by passionate employees. Alibaba founder Jack Ma went as far as calling it a "great blessing" in a 2019 essay, framing the grind as a necessary ingredient in the company's rise.

Some young Chinese have even left professional careers for lower-paying manual labor to escape the country's tough office culture. The surging youth unemployment rate suggests others are opting out entirely.

title: LAPD officer who recorded racist comments charged with eavesdropping
description: LAPD officer Daniel Flores was accused of making illegal recordings of his colleagues. The charges come after he filed a hostile workplace suit.
fullText:
A Los Angeles police officer who sued the city for a hostile work environment after he said colleagues made racist and discriminatory comments has been criminally charged for recording some of those comments.

Daniel Flores, 43, was charged with 16 felony counts of eavesdropping on or recording confidential communications, the Los Angeles District Attorney's Office announced on July 31.

The charges come weeks after Flores filed his lawsuit, which claimed he heard a supervisor and other colleagues working in the Los Angeles Police Department's Recruitment and Employment Division make derogatory comments based on race, national origin, gender or sexual orientation.

California is an all-party consent state, meaning that all people involved in a private conversation must consent to being audio recorded. In some states, only one person involved needs to consent, which means someone can legally record a conversation they are part of without the other person knowing.

LA top prosecutor Nathan J. Hochman gave a warning to anyone who records others without their knowledge, saying his office would prosecute "illegal eavesdroppers."

"It doesn't matter where you work or who you are – a neighbor, a co-worker or, in this case, a police officer. Your right to privacy in a confidential conversation is protected, no matter who is doing the recording or, with few exceptions, why they are doing the recording," Hochman said.

The recordings were made while Flores was assigned to the unit responsible for conducting background investigations for job candidates in 2024, Hochman's office said. "Some of the conversations allegedly included sexist, homophobic and racist remarks," the prosecutor's office acknowledged.

"We deplore the sexist, homophobic and racist remarks made by certain LAPD employees, and they should be held accountable for such statements. However ... one cannot simply choose to break the law because one wants to pursue a personal agenda," Hochman said.

What happened today? We make the long story short in this snappy news roundup

Flores could face up to 13 years in state prison if convicted. He is due in court on Aug. 10.

Flores' defense attorney, Alan Jackson, told USA TODAY in a statement that the officer plans to plead not guilty.

"Today the Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office charged a police officer with a crime for reporting racism inside the Los Angeles Police Department," Jackson said. "Not the officers who were recorded using racial, sexist, and anti-gay slurs. Not the officers who sat in a government building and said those things while holding the power to decide who becomes an LAPD officer. The officer who reported them."

Jackson said California's law about confidential communication doesn't apply when there is a reasonable expectation that a conversation could be overheard or recorded. He said the conversations took place in a public agency's workplace in front of colleagues.

Flores was acting in the scope of his duties as a police officer investigating misconduct, Jackson said.

"Officer Flores has served his city honorably. He told the truth. He will not apologize for it, and neither will we," he said.

According to a report by the Los Angeles Times, Flores turned in about 90 recordings to the LAPD's internal affairs department. An administrative investigation by the LAPD found him guilty of policy violations and recommended suspension without pay for 22 days, Flores' civil attorney Greg Smith told the Times; that disciplinary action has not yet been finalized.

LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell said in a statement that he supports the "legal process now underway."

"The LAPD's Internal Affairs Division conducted a thorough investigation, identified criminal conduct, and presented the facts for filing consideration, as is our responsibility when potential criminal conduct by an employee is discovered. I am committed to ensuring the workplace is professional, respectful, and free from misconduct, and any employee who violates those standards will be held accountable," McDonnell said in the statement.

In response to a USA TODAY inquiry, LAPD spokesperson Officer Jeff Lee said the department would not comment on pending litigation and was "prohibited from discussing personnel matters."

The recordings stirred up a wave of backlash against the police department when their existence was first reported on by the LA Times in 2025. Mayor Karen Bass said in a statement to KTLA at the time that the officers who made the comments were "stuck in the past."

"Growing LAPD's ranks is a top priority of this Administration and for our city's safety, so this conduct is especially outrageous and unacceptable," Bass said in 2025.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: LAPD officer who recorded racist comments charged with eavesdropping

title: Trump says Mideast allies have reached outlines of deal to end Iran war, says US to stop new strikes
description: President Donald Trump in a Saturday evening social media post claimed that Mideast allies have reached the parameters of a deal to end the Iran war and said that he would hold off on ordering new str...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump in a Saturday evening social media post claimed that Mideast allies have reached the parameters of a deal to end the Iran war and said that he would hold off on ordering new strikes in the five-month old conflict for now.

Trump added that the emerging deal "would include the Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran's nuclear threat."

"Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL," Trump said.

He said that Israel has agreed to join the U.S. in the commitment to try to complete the agreement with Iran that would bring about an end to the war.

Iran did not offer any immediate public reaction to Trump's announcement.

The president's announcement marked another remarkable turn in the conflict — only a day after he suggested to reporters that he was close to resuming heavy military strikes to force the regime to come to the negotiating table.

The U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, starting a war that Trump said was aimed at destroying Tehran's missile capabilities, preventing it from obtaining a nuclear weapon and ending its support for allied armed groups. But the stated goals and timelines for the conflict have repeatedly shifted.

An interim agreement reached in mid-June halted the fighting and was supposed to pave the way for a permanent deal, but it crumbled within weeks as Iran resumed attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Earlier Saturday, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the kingdom's de facto leader, in a phone call with Trump raised concerns about the U.S. potentially escalating the conflict with Iran, according to a person familiar with the leaders' discussion.

The discussion, which was first reported on by the news outlet Axios, came as Trump weighed whether to carry out new strikes on Iran.

The Saudis, according to the person briefed on the substance of the call but not authorized to comment publicly, are concerned that if the U.S. targets Iran's energy infrastructure or carries out massive strikes on bridges or power plants that Tehran could respond by carrying out attacks on the kingdom's and other Gulf countries' energy infrastructure.

The crown prince during Saturday's call sought clarity from Trump on what potential new action he's weighing to take against Iran, the person said.

A White House official, who was not authorized to comment publicly and requested anonymity, confirmed the leaders spoke on Saturday but did not offer any detail about their conversation.

Saudi Arabia earlier this week joined the U.S. in striking multiple logistics and weapons sites used by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq, but has been urging the U.S. and Iran to get back to the negotiating table to find an endgame to the conflict.

The crown prince also dispatched his brother, Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, to Washington on Wednesday for separate meetings with Trump and Vice President JD Vance to discuss Iran strategy.

And Trump met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday at the White House, their first in-person meeting since launching the war in February. The Israeli leader has urged Trump to continue to prosecute the war against Iran.

The stakes for continued U.S. military action are high for Trump and his party as the conflict, unpopular among many Americans, has jolted the world economy just months before critical midterm elections in November.

The president had vowed to take retaliatory action after the U.S. military thwarted a surprise attack earlier this week by Iran on a U.S. base in Jordan.

Trump on Friday displayed his growing frustration with the conflict, telling reporters that "we just want to win" in Iran and that the U.S. will hit Iran "very hard" until they can't take it anymore. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt echoed the president, noting that Tehran last month signed a memorandum of understanding with the U.S. on a truce but then quickly "broke it, shot at commercial ships, and killed American soldiers."

U.S. officials were on edge ahead of Trump's Saturday evening statement. And Trump himself in his social media post said that the U.S. military was "locked and loaded" and prepared to display "levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II."

Earlier in the day, the U.S. State Department issued new security alerts for Americans in 10 countries in the region to exercise heightened caution due to the escalating tensions with Iran.

The warnings — covering Bahrain, Israel, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and United Arab Emirates — urged U.S. citizens to prepare for the possibility of flight cancellations, temporary airspace closures and other travel disruptions.

Meanwhile, Kuwait's military said Saturday that its forces responded to drone attacks by Iran.

In a statement, Maj. Gen. Saud Abdulaziz Al-Otaibi, spokesperson for Kuwait's Defense Ministry, said the drones hit "a number of vital facilities," including a government structure in the country's north. He said there were no casualties.

The British Navy said Saturday that a tanker was struck and a separate explosion hit close to a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Oman. No casualties were reported in either incident, it said. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organization said an unknown projectile hit the vessel on Friday 11 nautical miles northeast of Lima, Oman. The attack damaged the vessel's engine room.

The group said that on Saturday a large splash and an explosion were reported close to another tanker while it was sailing 21 nautical miles northwest of Khasab city.

title: Trump’s Reflecting Pool debacle takes a predictably scandalous turn
description: Nothing about what happened Friday, when the Justice Department dropped its case against a purported Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool vandal, was completely surprising.
fullText:
Nothing about what happened Friday, when the Justice Department dropped its case against a purported Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool vandal, was completely surprising.

But that's also what makes it so scandalous.

The administration was pressed repeatedly about the possibility that the damage to the Reflecting Pool wasn't caused by vandals. Maybe it was just shoddy installation from the no-bid contractor that President Donald Trump hired. Maybe it was just a rushed job, reporters posited, given Trump wanted the pool ready for Independence Day celebrations.

But the administration has repeatedly and forcefully rejected these theories, straining to claim the damage was actually the work of radical-left vandals bent on destroying our country's precious monuments. It said this was proven and documented. And it eventually brought a high-profile case against someone – former Olympic canoeist David Hearn – who has spent that last month fending off a potential felony conviction.

Yet the Department of Justice moved to drop that case in typical Friday news-dump fashion, when many people have already tuned out for the weekend. And in doing so, it made some major admissions.

Basically, the DOJ said this was exactly what it seemed to be – that the damage "was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism."

Furthermore, it pointed the finger at the Department of Interior for willfully withholding information that would have demonstrated that fact and prevented the case from ever being brought.

"DOI provided less than fulsome information at the outset of this case," the DOJ said in its filing.

It added: "Had DOI been forthcoming with the information clearly in its possession, the government would not have sought a grand jury indictment."

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, for his part, argued on Saturday that the "evidence is clear" and that his department had provided the US attorney's office in Washington with "expert and eyewitness testimony to the damage done by vandals."

In normal times, all of that would be the stuff of major investigations and even congressional inquiries. According to Trump's own administration, other parts of the government withheld information, allowing for an unwarranted criminal case to be brought against an innocent man. And the DOJ brought a clearly shoddy case without getting all the information first.

And all, it bears emphasizing, while furthering Trump's political goals. Trump started claiming vandalism in mid-June after his coveted Reflecting Pool renovation began to quickly deteriorate – raising even more questions about his handling of the situation. It looks a lot like yet another hasty prosecution brought for Trump's political purposes has fallen apart.

Trump doubled down on the claim vandals damaged the pool after the DOJ move, writing on social media Saturday, "I disagree 100% with Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia, on the Reflecting Pool."

"I don't know what she was thinking? To me, it was a pure case of VANDALISM, that included the grass, which had a big 86 47 emblazoned in giant letters on it, and other elements of the surrounding area. There may have been some contractor difficulty, but the major damage was caused by VANDALS!" the president wrote on Truth Social, appearing to link the vandalism claim to the mysterious etching of "8647" that appeared on the grass of the National Mall in June.

But it's also worth just reflecting on how dishonestly and overzealously the administration prosecuted this case in public.

Over and over, it claimed things that have now been directly undermined by the new DOJ filing. And when pressed on alternative explanations that have now borne out, it flatly rejected them.

Shortly after Trump first raised the specter of vandals being responsible, a reporter in June asked him if it might just be the contractor's fault.

"No, no, vandals," Trump said, claiming they had cut a "300-foot slit" in the pool

When a reporter suggested it was odd that someone could vandalize the pool in such a way, given the "National Guard and police have been all over the Mall," Trump assured there was proof.

"I can't help it if somebody goes in with a knife and starts hacking it up," Trump added. "And we also have pictures of it."

Those pictures never arrived. (In fact, the DOJ didn't even accuse Hearn of using a sharp object.)

Trump went on to claim these were "thugs," "sick people," "people that want to destroy our country," "Radical Left SCUM that hate our Country" and "Country hating sleazebags." The length of the supposed slit in the pool gradually grew from 300 feet to 300 yards.

Hearn was eventually indicted on July 2. It was the only felony vandalism case, upgraded from a misdemeanor when the government claimed he caused at least $1,000 in damage. (The government also dropped at least two of the three misdemeanor charges it brought against other people.) And Pirro decided to hold a press conference.

When a reporter asked Pirro whether the pool was "probably damaged before" the Hearn incident, she repeatedly rejected the premise.

"Oh, he damaged it," Pirro said.

"But do you believe it had already been damaged before?" she was asked.

"He damaged the pool," Pirro said again.

"Before he touched it?" she was asked.

"He damaged the pool," she repeated.

In a later appearance on Fox News (where Pirro worked before becoming the DC US attorney), host Jesse Watters told Pirro, "A lot of people, when this first happened with the pool, didn't believe the president that there was vandalism."

"When these anarchists come – and we have witnesses – they're like, 'oh, we didn't do anything,'" she said, adding that the vandals act like "they have the right to destroy a monument."

"No, you don't," Pirro said emphatically.

A few days later, Burgum talked about the situation on the Sunday shows, with CNN's Dana Bash noting that the Reflecting Pool had already appeared to be peeling before Hearn arrived.

Burgum responded: "It didn't peel off. There was vandalism. There was box cutters."

"And you're 100% sure that what happened with the liner was vandalism? You can prove it?" Bash responded.

"Oh, yes absolutely, Dana," Burgum said.

Burgum went on: "I'm not sure why you and others in the media think that you want to keep trying to question whether or not … this is an industrial liner."

He added: "Literally, it would never just like peel off or fall off."

The Justice Department now says that Burgum's department was already in possession of information saying that's exactly what happened – that it had this information nearly a month earlier and withheld it.

"Almost immediately after work was initially completed, peeling was observed along the pool perimeter," the new DOJ filing said. "The NPS engineer's June 11, 2026, email stated that the cause of the damage was contractor error via 'overspray.'"

In the end, this appears to be exactly what it looked like in real time: A bunch of people straining to avoid the evidence right in front of their eyes in order to turn the president's politically expedient fantasy into a reality.

Even, it turns out, if it risked throwing an innocent man in prison.

This story was updated with additional information.

title: Man tries to build floating pub 'for a bit of fun'
description: Will Bower says the buoyant boozer is for his father, who loves "being on the water, and beer".
fullText:
The man behind a "lot of ridiculous stuff" has told the BBC he is trying to build a floating pub.

Will Bower, from Angmering in West Sussex, said he wants to create the buoyant boozer for his father's 60th birthday.

"[My dad] loves being on the water. He loves beer. I thought what better idea than to make a floating pub?" Bower said.

Bower plans to float the pub on the River Adur once he has finished building it.

He has purchased materials and building is currently under way.

"The dream is to float it somewhere and then have people with paddleboards or boats row up - and it's me and my dad there in sailor caps having a good time," he says.

Bower said after he designed the pub - which will sit on a floating pontoon - and purchased the materials, he struggled to find a mooring for it.

"There is a lot of red tape," he continued.

"A lot of people [were] saying... it's going to be too big. It's a step too far.

"[I am going] to prove them wrong."

Arun District Council, who Bower had requested permission from, said: "While it's certainly a creative idea and we appreciate the imagination, our ponds and lakes are relatively modest in size and not suitable for testing a floating pub due to safety and environmental concerns.

"We wish Will every success in getting his venture afloat at a more suitable location," it added.

Owing to issues with getting permission, Bower now plans to float the pub on the tidal River Adur - between Upper Beeding and Shoreham-by-Sea - where the public has a right of navigation.

Bower, a YouTuber, says he has built other "ridiculous stuff", including a bath car and a fake skip in Worthing High Street which he slept in.

"The skip was fun," he told the BBC.

"The hypothesis was that skips are the most invisible things in Britain."

Bower added that the night on Worthing High Street was a "little bit sketchy", although he said he enjoyed it.

"At one point a bin lorry pulled up right next to it and I thought I was going to get thrown in the back."

Bower says people "absolutely love" his creations, such as when he drives his bath car around his home town.

"Hopefully the pub can brighten someone's day."

title: Body of missing 10-year-old girl found in Passaic River in NJ
description: A 10-year-old girl’s body was recovered from New Jersey’s Passaic River after a two-day search.
fullText:
The body of a 10-year-old girl who went missing after being swept into New Jersey's Passaic River was found July 31 after a two-day search, officials said.

Passaic Mayor Hector Lora said crews recovered the girl's body in the river south of the Market Street Bridge shortly before 7 p.m. Friday, July 31. The child was identified as Milian Dulan, according to PIX11.

The discovery came after emergency crews searched nearly 9 miles of the Passaic River using boats, sonar equipment, drones, helicopters and cadaver dogs. The search began July 29 after three children entered the water near a boat ramp at Pulaski Park in Passaic, New Jersey, and were swept away by the current.

One child, an 11-year-old girl, was able to get out of the river on her own, officials said. The bodies of her 10-year-old brother, identified by PIX11 as Michael Klenk, and Dulan were later recovered, officials said.

Authorities were preparing to end the search for the night Friday when a couple living near the Market Street Bridge reported seeing something in the river from their apartment window, CBS News reported.

The couple went outside to investigate and called 911 after believing they had seen the missing child's body. Officials said rescue boats were deployed within about 15 minutes and recovered Dulan approximately 100 feet from the bridge in Wallington, New Jersey.

Lora praised the couple for alerting authorities, saying their quick response may have prevented the body from being carried farther downstream by the river's strong current.

"Had that couple not said anything, and the current, as fast and as strong as it was, would've continued all night, there could be a possibility [the body] would've ended up by the Newark Bay," Lora told CBS News.

The girl's mother was brought to the scene and identified her daughter, officials said. Lora said the family experienced both grief and some comfort after receiving confirmation.

Officials said the children were from Garfield, New Jersey, though one family has ties to Passaic. The children were playing near the riverbank at Pulaski Park before ending up on a boat ramp normally used by police and fire crews.

A good Samaritan at the park attempted to enter the river to rescue the children but was unable to reach them because of the river's depth and strong current, Lora said.

The search operation included more than two dozen marine units from local, county and state agencies, along with dive teams and other emergency responders.

Reporter Anthony Thompson can be reached at ajthompson@usatodayco.com, or on X @athompsonUSAT

title: ‘More than just objects’: Australian booksellers raise alarm over ‘horrific’ destruction of rare titles to feed AI
description: Secondhand booksellers believe they may have been caught up in the AI supply chain that sees old books scanned then...
fullText:
Secondhand booksellers believe they may have been caught up in the AI supply chain that sees old books scanned then destroyed

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

“Sometimes books tell you more than the content,” says Tim White, as he lines up carefully dust-jacketed books and pamphlets in plastic sleeves on temporary shelves in Melbourne University’s Wilson Hall.

He’s preparing his stall for this weekend’s Melbourne Rare Book Fair. For people like White, who runs independent bookshop Books for Cooks, the book as a physical object is just as important as what’s inside it.

“We’re interested in where food and society connect … So we just keep pushing the boundaries, looking for things that show unusual aspects of that, things that tell us a bit more about what it is to be human,” he says.

“That’s what most of us [rare booksellers] do. We handle things that have a story.”

But vendors and rare books experts are increasingly worried that these artefacts may be under threat of destruction by generative AI companies seeking to feed their ravenous technology with new texts.

Fears stem from a copyright lawsuit brought against AI company Anthropic in the United States by book authors. Unsealed court files revealed earlier this year that the company was engaging in the practice of “destructive scanning” – buying physical books, slicing off the spines to more efficiently scan the pages, then pulping the remains – and had sought to keep it quiet. The judge ruled this was lawful under US copyright law, as it amounted to “transformative use”.

The practice is now understood to be widespread among generative AI companies, and recent reports suggest intermediaries are stepping up to facilitate the process. Australian secondhand booksellers are wondering if they have been caught up in the AI supply chain after they recently experienced waves of orders that did not fit with usual customer patterns.

Multiple vendors confirmed to Guardian Australia they had received orders from a Canadian company called Zoom Books, which describes itself as a book recycler. The orders usually came through large secondhand marketplaces like Abebooks or Biblio, where inventory can range from cheap paperbacks to rare, expensive items.

Delfina Manor, who runs Good Reading Secondhand Books in Benalla, Victoria, said she received orders from Zoom Books in May amounting to three full boxes, but had to write to the company and ask them not to order in such volume again.

“They ordered, paid in advance, and they didn’t quibble over the postage … [but] it would have been about 30 to 40 books, and so finding them, packing them, making sure you hadn’t missed one out … It was just driving me nuts,” Manor said.

John Sainsbury, owner of Melbourne’s Sainsburys Books, confirmed a slew of orders from Zoom Books had come through the store’s online listings around the same time. The orders were price insensitive and appeared entirely random – niche titles, “bottom-end” and sometimes decades-old stock. The orders resulted in Sainsburys shipping multiple boxes overseas.

Sainsbury described his company as “a general bookseller at an antiquarian book fair”, as he doesn’t just deal in rare material. The profile fits the pattern of vendors who have received similar orders – high-end specialist sellers did not appear to have been approached.

Some vendors speculated the company may be buying the books on arbitrage – common enough in the secondhand book trade – but the specific requests nevertheless seemed odd. In one order, a 1970s manual on soil mechanics was bought alongside a 2010 book called Born to Thunder: Champions of New Zealand Cycling, a collection of Early Australian Poetry (1982), and a local history of the Melbourne suburb of Hawthorn. The poetry book sold for $9 and had been on the shelf for 20 years.

White says the issue raises “an interesting tension”. “If it’s a $20 book of which there’s … 500,000 copies in Australia, I wouldn’t cry,” he says. “I’d have different issues around copyright.”

“If it’s a book that has that storytelling element to it, or it’s a one-off, it’s horrific.”

For booksellers struggling to catalogue their vast stock of books, let alone sell them, such sales aren’t necessarily bad.

Nick Dawes, who runs Grant’s Bookshop with his wife, Jenny, estimates they have about 500,000 books in their warehouses.

“If somebody wanted to come and buy all my books and cut them up, well … I’d be unhappy at one level, but I’d be happy at another,” says Dawes. “But if somebody said to me, look, this is the only known copy, I’m going to cut it up, then I’d say, I think I’d rather not send it to you.”

AI companies are not the first to destroy books for profit. Some vendors source rare books in order to slice them up and sell the illustration plates individually.

“When I sell a book and then find the prints available individually, I just find it physically abhorrent,” says rare bookseller Gwenyth Todd from Chatelaine Books. She screens buyers accordingly, so the books don’t go “to the wrong home”.

“To me books are more than just objects.”

An Anthropic spokesperson said the company has never bought from Zoom Books, but that “sourcing books is a widely used approach for training large language models across the AI industry”. Anthropic procures its books from mainstream commercial markets, the spokesperson said. “None of our data acquisition programs buy and destroy rare or antiquarian books.”

Zoom Books’ co-founder, Manroop Gill, said in a recent LinkedIn post that the company had been “expanding aggressively” in the past months.

Zoom Books has previously denied it destructively scans books. A spokesperson told Guardian Australia: “We acquire secondhand books and resell them intact. We do not digitize books. Our priority is always reuse, and when a book can no longer be rehomed, it is responsibly recycled.”

The company did not disclose if it sold intact books to AI companies for destructive scanning, saying: “Our commercial agreements require confidentiality, so we do not disclose or discuss our customers.”

title: ‘The language of Pokémon is universal’: why fans are still catching ‘em all after 30 years
description:
As Pokémon Go celebrates its 10th anniversary, its devoted players explain how the game has created a vibrant intergenerational community spanning the globe
Most Pokémon obsessives count rare, absurdly expensive playing cards or pristine, fully boxed game cartridges that have survived decades in the attic among their most prized possessions. But for Mairead Ralph, her Pokémon-related crown jewel is a bit different. “Technically, it’s my husband!” she says.
The pair first locked eyes amid decks of Pokémon playing cards and Pokéballs at a fan event 16 years ago and the rest is history.
fullText:
As Pokémon Go celebrates its 10th anniversary, its devoted players explain how the game has created a vibrant intergenerational community spanning the globe

Most Pokémon obsessives count rare, absurdly expensive playing cards or pristine, fully boxed game cartridges that have survived decades in the attic among their most prized possessions. But for Mairead Ralph, her Pokémon-related crown jewel is a bit different. “Technically, it’s my husband!” she says.

The pair first locked eyes amid decks of Pokémon playing cards and Pokéballs at a fan event 16 years ago and the rest is history. Ralph was among hundreds of Pokémon fans who flocked to Shoreditch, east London, on Saturday afternoon for a pop-up celebrating the 10th anniversary of Pokémon Go, the massively successful augmented reality smartphone game that has seen millions of players physically venture to all corners of the earth to catch ’em all in person. In that spirit, the surrounding area was full of Pokéheads wandering the streets, their heads in their phones, seeking to catch exclusive Pokémon that had been released.

Ralph, 42, is an OG Pokémon fan, getting into Pokémon Red when the game (and franchise) debuted 30 years ago. “I’ve been in love with it ever since,” she says. Months after Pokémon Red released in Japan in February 1996, the now-famous playing cards were released, some of which have since soared in value to thousands or even millions of pounds. Earlier this year, the world’s only Professional Sports Authenticator (PSA) 10-graded Pikachu Illustrator card was sold for a staggering £12m.

The franchise, which spans video games, playing cards, TV shows, films and merchandise, has become so big that the Pokémon company, which celebrated its 30th birthday in March, is now the world’s biggest media franchise, with total revenues of $147bn (£110bn), according to Guinness World Records.

This is far from the first Pokémon-related event Ralph has attended. She has travelled to Japan, the US and France to mingle with fellow fans. Despite often not sharing the same language, this hasn’t been a challenge for Ralph. “The language of Pokémon is universal,” she says.

Ralph even met her husband at one event. “I was at an event doing Pokémon stuff and he was working in a different area, and then we ran into each other at the local nerdy shop,” she says. Their love of the franchise extended to their wedding. Instead of having numbered tables, they had Pokémon. “If you were told to join Pikachu’s friends, you had to find the table with his face on it,” she says.

She thinks Pokémon has remained popular because it “brings people back to a happy place, no matter how bad the world is”, especially during these tricky times where issues such as the cost of living are hitting hard. It helps that most Pokémon are “happy and smiley” apart from a few “grumpy” outliers. “I’m looking at you, Mewtwo,” she says.

Also at the pop-up was Rumeysa Usca and her animated pomeranian Boomi. The 34-year-old engineer travelled from Leamington to attend the event. For her, the appeal of Pokémon Go is simple. “I can entertain my dog, entertain myself and lose weight,” she says. Usca has been playing the smartphone game for four years and has been a lifelong fan of the franchise, which she attributes to it “never having a break”, with new products being regularly released.

She also says Pokémon taps into nostalgia and a desire to return to simpler times. “As kids, we were so happy watching and playing it. It just brings back those good emotions,” Usca says.

Summer Till, 24, says it’s a good way to connect with younger relatives. “There’s a generation gap between me and my niece and nephew, but Pokémon is common ground for us,” she says.

Those who wanted a free coffee with a branded Pokémon Go cup needed to complete a challenge on the game along the surrounding streets. Among those taking part was Stacie Smith and her son Rupert. They travelled in from Southend in Essex. “She’s been getting all the luck,” says Rupert, referring to his mum catching better Pokémon than him on her phone. Smith remembers collecting Pokémon cards when she was growing up. “We would buy them along with panini stickers and Spice Girls postcards,” she says. And she then became fond of the cartoon, which was a staple on children’s TV in the late 1990s. Rupert enjoys the playing cards aspect more, but the pair have found a “shared love” of the franchise through Pokémon Go.

Rupert has autism, which means he “doesn’t like leaving the house very much”, says Smith, but the game has encouraged him to start venturing outside more, and the pair spend more time together. This, she says, is “really important for his mental health and trying to get him integrated into communities so he can talk to other people”.

At school, he’s made friends through his enthusiasm for Pokémon. He’s been handed down some Pokémon cards from family, including a first-edition holo Mewtwo from his dad. If kept in pristine, PSA 10-graded condition, the card could fetch about £18,000, but with a few bends and tears Rupert’s has been well-loved and is sadly less valuable.

But for many in attendance, their love of the franchise is hardly material. Ralph’s love of Pokémon will be enduring. “It doesn’t matter if it’s your first Pokémon or your thousandth Pokémon, that little click of the Pokéball will always bring you joy.”

title: GB win two more golds at European Aquatics Championships
description: Great Britain win golds in the women's synchronised 10m diving and artistic swimming mixed duet at the European Aquatics Championships in Paris.
fullText:
Great Britain won golds in the women's synchronised 10m diving and artistic swimming mixed duet at the European Aquatics Championships in Paris.

Maisie Bond and Lois Toulson achieved a score of 300.06 to clinch the women's 10m - just ahead of second-placed Germany (298.20) and Ukraine (286.20) in third.

"We came into these championships wanting to win and knowing it was possible," said Toulson. "We'd been training really hard and looking good I think.

"That was a [personal best] for us. To be able to do that and get a gold medal - we're really proud."

In the mixed duet, Isabelle Thorpe and Ranjuo Tomblin narrowly claimed their first European title in the event.

The pair won with a score of 258.2383 as they beat Spain by just 0.2650 to take victory, with Italy (255.1641) in third.

"It's incredible. I'm really happy and to have done it with Ranjuo is incredible." said Olympic silver medallist Thorpe.

"We didn't have the most smooth sailing preparation due to injury, but it's good we have been able to come through it and be on top."

Tomblin, who defended his title in the men's solo technical event on Friday, added: "Today is more special because I get to do it with Izzy, so it's incredible."

In the men's 1m springboard diving final, Jack Laugher claimed silver with a score of 418.25 and fellow Briton Jordan Houlden took bronze with 410.30 as they finished behind winner Germany Moritz Linus Wesemann (431.45).

title: 'Future of tour' Eala beats Osaka to reach Washington final
description: Alexandra Eala continues her strong season with an impressive victory over Naomi Osaka to reach the Washington Open final.
fullText:
Alexandra Eala continued her strong season with an impressive victory over Naomi Osaka to reach the Washington Open final.

The Filipina beat Japan's four-time major champion Osaka 6-4 6-2 to set up a final against world number three Jessica Pegula.

Eala began the year outside the world's top 50 but will now rise to a career high of 24th in the rankings.

The 21-year-old has registered six wins over top-10 players this season, including ending Iga Swiatek's Wimbledon title defence in July.

Eala became the first singles player from the Philippines to reach the fourth round of a major in the Open era with her Wimbledon run, and has developed a passionate fanbase.

In Washington, Eala beat second seed Elina Svitolina and 2025 champion Leylah Fernandez before sweeping past Osaka as she bids for a first WTA Tour title.

American Pegula described Eala as "the future of the tour" before their final on Sunday.

Dog walk and expletive text - key findings in Vondrousova anti-doping case

Norrie beaten by Shapovalov in Los Cabos semi-final

Pegula won their previous meeting, a tight three-set match in the Miami Open semi-finals last year.

However, Eala has improved since then, notably on her serve. She won 71% of first-serve points against Osaka, and dropped only four points behind her second.

"I'm more well-rounded [now]. I'm physically a little bit better," Eala said.

"I played really well, had a great mentality and stayed locked in until the end."

Pegula came back from 5-2 down in the first set to beat Russia's Diana Shnaider 7-5 6-4 and reach a second Washington final.

In the men's tournament, third seed Taylor Fritz will face rising Spanish star Rafael Jodar in the final.

World number 10 Fritz hit 13 aces to beat fellow American Brandon Nakashima 6-3 3-6 6-3.

Jodar - who will break into the world's top 20 after starting the year ranked 165th - beat Chile's Alejandro Tabilo 6-7 (6-8) 6-4 6-4.

title: What happened to star signings your club never made?
description: BBC Sport takes a look at some star players who were close to moving to the Premier League, only for the deals to fall through.
fullText:
Fans always get excited when the transfer window comes around.

Your team is linked with a big-name signing and you start to dream they could be the ones to lead your club to glory.

Tottenham fans might have felt this way a few years ago when they were strongly linked with a young, prolific striker from Nigeria by the name of Gift Orban.

They had every reason, on paper at least, to be excited.

In the summer of 2023, Orban, then 21, was regarded as one of the hottest prospects in the game.

After scoring 16 goals in 22 games for Norwegian top-flight side Stabaek, he moved to Belgian side Gent and continued his impressive goalscoring record, netting 20 times in 22 matches.

In a wild four-day period in March 2023, he scored seven goals in two matches. He got four in a 6–2 away league win over Zulte Waregem, becoming the first Gent player with a four-goal haul in one game in the 21st Century.

He then followed up with a quick-fire hat-trick in a 4–1 away victory over Istanbul Basaksehir in the Conference League last 16.

That hat-trick was completed within three minutes and 25 seconds, at the time a record in Uefa club competitions.

With England captain Harry Kane set to join Bayern Munich later that summer, Tottenham needed a striker.

Orban was even touted in the BBC Gossip Column as the club's Kane replacement. The headline of a follow-up story read: "Could Orban be a global star?"

However, Spurs, with new boss Ange Postecoglou recently appointed, stalled at the £25m fee and the move collapsed.

In the three years since, Orban has had four clubs, most recently joining newly-promoted Turkish top-flight side Amedspor on loan last week.

He has struggled to regain his form with only three goals for Gent in 2023-24, three for French side Lyon and four for Bundesliga outfit Hoffenheim, although he scored seven times in Serie A on loan at Verona last season.

While his career is yet to reach the heights it once promised, other missed transfer targets have had rather different outcomes...

In January 2009, newly-rich Manchester City were looking to spend a bit of their bulging bank balance to sign Brazilian playmaker Kaka.

AC Milan and Kaka's heads were turned by City's staggering £108m offer, which would have been more than double the world record transfer at the time.

One City fan was so sure the deal would be done that he apparently got the playmaker's name tattooed on his chest., external

However, in the end, the 2007 Ballon d'Or winner decided the timing wasn't right and turned down the chance to move to Manchester.

Kaka did make a world-record move later in 2009, joining Real Madrid for £56m six months later.

He won the Spanish Cup in 2011 and La Liga the following year before one season back at AC Milan.

He then spent three years at Major League Soccer side Orlando City before ending his playing career back in his homeland with Sao Paulo.

In 2004, Bolton Wanderers were flying high, with dreams of Europe.

Manager Sam Allardyce went big, with an enquiry for 32-year-old Brazilian World Cup winner Rivaldo, who had been frozen out at AC Milan.

Rivaldo himself made a statement, saying: "I want the challenge of trying to get Bolton into Europe for the first time in their history. It is an exciting time."

In the end, he had a change of heart and went to Greek side Olympiakos instead, where he stayed for three seasons.

Bolton finished that 2004-05 campaign in sixth - tied on points with Liverpool and just three points off the top four. That earned them a place in Uefa Cup qualifying, and they went on to reach the last 32.

After Olympiakos, Rivaldo had spells with AEK Athens, then in Uzbekistan and Angola before returning to Brazil.

In 1995, Blackburn Rovers had just won the Premier League title and turned down the chance to sign a young French midfielder, Zinedine Zidane from Bordeaux.

Club management urged owner Jack Walker to buy Zidane and France forward Christophe Dugarry, but Walker famously replied: "Why do we need Zidane when we have Tim Sherwood?"

Sherwood had lifted the Premier League trophy a few months earlier and both Zidane and Dugarry had flown to England to talk to the club but no deal was completed.

Zidane and Dugarry went on to win the World Cup with France in 1998 and the European Championship two years later, with Zidane lifting two Italian titles with Juventus and then La Liga and the Champions League with Real Madrid.

Dugarry had spells at AC Milan, Barcelona, Marseille and back at Bordeaux, although he did end his career in England with two seasons at Birmingham City.

In 2005, just off the back of a sensational Champions League win when Liverpool fought back from 3-0 down at half-time against AC Milan before winning on penalties, Steven Gerrard upset the red half of Merseyside. He handed in a transfer request.

Chelsea boss Jose Mourinho was interested in acquiring the England midfielder's services in a potential £32m move, with Gerrard refusing to sign a new contract.

Eventually Gerrard decided to stay with Liverpool, citing "family reasons". Gerrard would go on to make more than 700 appearances for the Reds and guide them to the 2007 Champions League final, although AC Milan would get their revenge.

Ten years later, Mourinho said his failure to sign Gerrard was one of his greatest transfer disappointments.

France striker Kylian Mbappe is the record goalscorer in World Cups, helping his country win the 2018 competition and then scoring a hat-trick in the 2022 final as Les Bleus lost on penalties to Argentina.

However, he could have been a Liverpool player in 2017 as he had talks with the Reds when still at Monaco.

"I talked to Liverpool because it's the favourite club of my mum, my mum loves Liverpool," said Mbappe.

Then-Liverpool boss Jurgen Klopp recently revealed how the club laid on a private jet and food for Mbappe and his family.

However, despite his mother's favourite club being the Reds, Mbappe joined Paris St-Germain, where he won six successive Ligue 1 titles before joining Real Madrid in 2024.

France striker Antoine Griezmann has had a great career, but never played in the Premier League.

But he nearly did, with Fulham making an unlikely £12m bid for him in January 2014 when the Cottagers were fighting to stay in the Premier League.

Fulham enquired about Griezmann to his club Real Sociedad and were quoted a price of £12m. In the end, the west London side spent that figure on Olympiakos striker Kostas Mitroglou, who only played three Premier League matches, scoring no goals, before the Cottagers were relegated.

Mitroglou then had loan spells back at Olympiakos and then Benfica, who he joined permanently in 2016-17.

Griezmann stayed in Spain with nine seasons over two spells at Atletico Madrid and two years at Barcelona. He helped France win the World Cup in 2018.

title: New boss Maresca is perfect for Man City - Gvardiol
description: New manager Enzo Maresca is a "perfect one" for Manchester City, says defender Josko Gvardiol.
fullText:
New manager Enzo Maresca is a "perfect one" for Manchester City, says defender Josko Gvardiol.

The Italian has been given the perhaps unenviable task of taking over from the legendary Pep Guardiola, who stepped down at the end of last season after a trophy-laden decade in charge.

Maresca signed a three-year deal to succeed the Spaniard, having previously won the Championship title with Leicester and the Club World Cup with Chelsea.

The 46-year-old took charge of City for the first time in Saturday's friendly defeat on penalties by Inter Milan in Hong Kong.

"The level is that high and he has been chosen with reason as the manager," said Gvardiol.

"I think he has a quality, has some new ideas and also we need to see what we are going to do [with] the style of [play], the football we are going to play and the tactics.

"I think he is a perfect one, but of course, it takes time. It's something totally new, it's not easy to change the manager, so we will take time.

"It's our job to help him as much as possible and also to listen to try to adapt as quick as possible.

"I met him, we spoke a little bit about my injury [and] also how we played, how I played before with Pep, and that's it, more or less."

McAidoo 'the kind of winger I love' - Maresca

Man City staying in world's 'best hotel' on pre-season tour

Gvardiol missed five months of last season after sustaining a broken bone in his right leg in January, before returning to play twice in May.

There had been speculation throughout the campaign that Guardiola could leave and signs pointed at an exit, before the manager finally confirmed his decision in the last week of the season.

"Some would say he could have told us earlier, some would say not," said Gvardiol.

"I think it was perfect timing because it can affect you mentally if he would have said it earlier.

"We knew at some point he has to tell us. He has been here for 10 years and it is time to rest a little bit and retire. We could feel it.

"[The 2024-25 season] he was in between, about to leave, then he stayed - great because it was another season to try to win something. Two seasons ago we struggled, 13 games without winning.

"Unfortunately it was time [for him] to go but who knows with him, maybe after six months when he gets the energy back."

Gvardiol played all four games at this summer's World Cup as Croatia suffered an agonising last-32 defeat by Portugal, seeing a late equaliser ruled out by the video assistant referee.

City team-mate Ruben Dias featured for Portugal in that game, while midfielder Rodri captained Spain to World Cup glory.

Both players are candidates to take the armband at City following the departure of Bernardo Silva, who left to join Real Madrid upon the expiry of his contract, while experienced defender John Stones has joined Inter on a free.

Gvardiol, meanwhile, will extend his stay at Etihad Stadium after signing a new five-year deal last week.

Asked about the club's leadership group, Gvardiol said: "It's difficult to tell you about this but we need to see.

"Ruben is one of the leaders in our team and he is probably going to be on the top now - maybe the most important one.

"He will need some guys who have been here for a longer time. So if that's on me, I will take responsibility."

title: A bruising 24 hours - what next for Fifa and under-pressure Infantino?
description: The pressure is building on Gianni Infantino. Can he survive as Fifa president?
fullText:
A week is a long time in politics. Football politics.

On Tuesday morning, Gianni Infantino was in an impregnable position as Fifa president, the most powerful job in football.

Now, after trying to sell stakes in Fifa competitions to private investments firms - apparently without the knowledge of anyone else - Infantino's position appears to be under threat.

Uefa - Infantino's fiercest critic - dealt its trump card on Thursday by threatening to boycott all Fifa competitions, including the World Cup.

Now European football's governing body senses the opportunity to remove Infantino - and this is likely to be the best chance it will ever get.

But they're far from the only unhappy federation.

Concacaf, the confederation Infantino worked so closely with to organise the 2026 World Cup, has called for a "full review" into the leadership of Fifa in light of Infantino's plan.

Even more damaging, loyal countries in the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) shunned him too.

Then he was abandoned by two of his closest allies - first senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro and then chief operating officer Kevin Lamour.

After Infantino backtracked in the early hours of Saturday morning, Uefa delivered another devastating blow by issuing a strong statement saying it had lost confidence in him.

The battles lines have been drawn. What could happen next?

Uefa has 'lost confidence' in Infantino's Fifa leadership

Four reasons why Fifa's World Cup plan never stacked up

Infantino on the brink? Who might replace him if he goes?

The quickest route for Infantino's exit would be for the Swiss to resign, like his predecessor Sepp Blatter did in 2015.

But Infantino still retains support and he could try to hold out until March, when he is up for re-election for a fourth and final term as president.

The Fifa Council could try to force Infantino's hand through an emergency meeting.

Such a gathering would be triggered if 19 of the 37 Fifa Council members call for one.

Uefa has nine members, AFC has seven, Concacaf five, Africa has six, Conmebol five and Oceania three. It is completed by Infantino and secretary general Mattias Grafstrom.

BBC Sport understands there are some doubts that the 19 votes could be achieved.

If they do get to 19, the meeting must take place within two weeks and the Fifa Council could call on Infantino to tender his resignation. But he could simply refuse to do so.

It would, however, add further pressure.

The next step would be an extraordinary congress of the 211 Fifa member associations, which would be held if one-fifth, or 43 associations, "make such a request in writing".

So Uefa, which has 55 nations, can trigger the extraordinary congress whenever it so wishes.

That would take a minimum of two months from the point it is triggered, but more likely three months, and there is no guarantee of success.

In effect, it would be a de facto election without there being another candidate as 106 votes would be needed to pass the vote of no confidence.

Uefa has 55, Africa 54, Asia 46, Concacaf 35, Oceania 11 and Conmebol 10.

Africa, Conmebol and Oceania have not criticised Infantino's plan.

So could Uefa get to 106? In total, 136 countries officially rejected the investment plan, but voting to reject an idea is not the same as voting to kick Infantino out.

Of the 136, Qatar have already publicly backed him and Mexico have distanced themselves from the joint Concacaf statement.

Which leaves finding a suitable candidate to fight the election in March.

Infantino stood unopposed when he was re-elected in 2019 and 2023 and if someone wants to battle him for the position, the deadline to announce their candidacy is 18 November.

The five dramatic days that shook Infantino and world football

If Uefa and Infantino's biggest critics have to go down the election route, they will need to find a unifying leader.

As Uefa has been so strong in its opposition to Infantino, a European candidate might struggle to get global support. After all, it might seem like it is trying to take over Fifa itself.

So there must be a candidate who can attract the support of those countries in Concacaf, Africa and Asia who could have been loyal to Infantino but could be persuaded to switch their votes.

The most likely candidate appears to be Concacaf president Victor Montagliani.

Like Infantino, he was elected in 2016 promising governance reform. A former president of Canada Soccer, Montagliani was heavily involved in the build up to and delivery of the 2026 World Cup. He is fluent in French, Italian and Spanish, as well as English.

Another option would be Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa, the AFC president.

Initially elected in 2013, he was re-elected unopposed for a fourth term to run to 2027.

Sheikh Salman signed off the confederation's brutal takedown of how Fifa is being run by Infantino and has carried with him a 46-member confederation, many of whom are aware the figures being offered by Infantino's plan are huge in terms of their overall football expenditure.

Less likely appears to be Paris St-Germain president Nasser Al-Khelaifi, the Qatari who is also the chair of European Football Clubs.

Al-Khelaifi helped bring European football back together after another seismic event that threatened to pull the game apart - the ill-fated European Super League.

In theory, the Qatari would be a serious challenger to Infantino. But it seems he doesn't want the role. Qatar's support for Infantino could be an issue, too.

In any other business, Infantino would be unlikely to continue in his role.

But football, of course, is not a normal business.

Remember Sepp Blatter, who resigned in 2015 when he had no option left amid a corruption scandal. He had even been re-elected the week before.

So will Infantino try to fight on?

In his statement on Saturday, he said his intent "was to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks".

For Infantino, contrition could make this all float away.

Maybe it is working. Following on from Qatar, 2030 co-hosts Morocco backed him on Saturday evening. Then Egypt praised Infantino for cancelling his masterplan.

Infantino may be thinking that if he can, day by day, get more member associations on board, the prospect of a vote of no confidence is less likely to be successful.

After all, his support base has been so strong for so long you can understand why he might have such confidence.

As a vote of no confidence is three months away, he has the chance to repair at least some of the damage.

It is a race to 106 - and the more time elapses, the more chance Infantino can persuade his former allies this was just an aberration.

For Uefa, the question is whether it can create a situation whereby Infantino is left with no option but to resign.

For that to happen, the criticism from federations across the world must continue.

But if there is one thing that could damage Infantino further, it would be for major sponsors to distance themselves from the organisation.

During the 2015 Fifa scandal, Sony, Emirates, Castrol, Continental Tyres and Johnson & Johnson were among the companies to discontinue their huge sponsorship deals.

There is no sign of this just yet but this is a saga with the potential to rumble on.

title: Mets prospect Jonathan Santucci strikes out seven in Triple-A debut
description: Mets top pitching prospect Jonathan Santucci made his Triple-A debut Saturday evening and struck out seven across four-plus innings against Rochester.
fullText:
Mets top pitching prospect Jonathan Santucci made his Triple-A debut Saturday evening and while he showed his overpowering stuff, it was a grind for the left-hander.

Going up against Rochester, Santucci allowed two runs on five hits and five walks while striking out seven.

Santucci's night started with back-to-back walks, and he eventually walked the bases loaded but got Andrew Pinckney to ground out into an inning-ending double play to get out of the jam.

The second inning saw Santucci not walk a batter, but a leadoff single and a two-out triple gave Rochester the early 1-0 lead. The next batter hit a double to push across the second run charged to Santucci, but that would be all he would give up. Santucci's third inning saw him strike out three batters, working around a two-out double before stranding a runner on second in the fourth inning.

Santucci started the fifth, but after a six-pitch walk, the southpaw was pulled.

Overall, Santucci tossed 90 pitches (52 strikes) in his four-plus innings of work. A solid start for Santucci, who could be fast-tracked to the majors if his development continues. He was promoted to Syracuse on July 28 after overpowering Double-A. Although his ERA sat at 3.57, he was mowing down the competition, striking out 120 batters across 90.2 innings (19 starts).

title: Iman Shumpert disagrees with Shaquille O'Neal about the 76ers' title favorite status
description: Shaquille O'Neal is adamant that the 76ers are championship-or-bust in the 2026-27 season.
fullText:
Iman Shumpert disagrees with Shaquille O'Neal about the 76ers' title favorite status originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

With the additions of LeBron James and Jaylen Brown to the Philadelphia 76ers' roster, they are now being called one of the favorites to win the 2027 championship. It is fair to have those expectations because adding two Finals MVPs to the roster is a massive boost for the team's chances.

The players who were already in Philly beforehand are happy with the additions. In fact, they actively recruited James to the team, which is a good sign for the team's culture because it seems everyone wants to learn from the four-time Finals MVP, including sophomore guard VJ Edgecombe.

It is easy for people to get ahead of themselves when it comes to discussing championship favorites. That has been normal basketball discourse over the years, but crowning the 76ers is too early, especially with all kinds of elite teams throughout the league.

Shaquille O'Neal believes that this is a championship-or-bust season for the 76ers. Those are some extremely high expectations, but it seems he believes the 76ers can finally end their title drought, especially with LeBron as the biggest name on the team.

MORE: Iman Shumpert believes LeBron James appreciates the challenge of leading the 76ers to a title

Considering the New York Knicks are the defending champions, they will have something to say about this. Iman Shumpert has disagreed with O'Neal because he does not want to count out Jalen Brunson and the Knicks, as they are ready to defend their championship.

"Jalen Brunson leads the fourth quarter scoring for the past five consecutive years. Look, Tyrese (Maxey), I love you to death, but you have to show me you can beat Jalen Brunson... Jalen Brunson needs to be stopped before we start considering others for a championship," Shumpert said on Shaq's The Big Podcast.

Shumpert brings up a great point because branding the 76ers' upcoming season as a championship-or-bust campaign means O'Neal sees them as the favorite. With the Knicks, the San Antonio Spurs, and the Oklahoma City Thunder all present in the league, this makes it hard for the 76ers to be the favorites.

title: Luka Doncic’s Offseason Transformation Has Lakers Fans Excited
description: Lakers star Luka Doncic is in Europe this offseason, spending time with his daughters while rehabilitating from his hamstring injury. The post Luka Doncic’s Offseason Transformation Has Lakers Fans Excited appeared first on LA Sports Report.
fullText:
Los Angeles Lakers star Luka Doncic is in Europe this offseason, spending time with his daughters while rehabilitating from his hamstring injury.

Doncic missed the entire postseason and the end of the regular season after his left hamstring tore.

Despite talk about Doncic possibly coming back in time for the playoffs, the Slovenian and the Lakers decided against being irresponsible and held him out.

He has been a star for years, but Doncic is only 27 years old, and the organization was intent on protecting his long-term future, which LA hopes will be in purple and gold.

While he takes time out for his family and to reset, Doncic is not leaving basketball in the rearview mirror. In fact, he looks to be in sensational shape.

The Lakers’ official X account posted a photo of Doncic with a new fashion accessory, looking to be in sensational shape, even better than last offseason.

Lakers fans are taking notice of his shape and new look, and to say they are excited would be an understatement.

“hes going to tear it up next season, this team has multiple ball handlers and playmaking. he wont need to play a full 1st quarter to start the game and can manage his minutes thru out the game,” one user commented under the Lakers’ post.

“Damn Headband Luka looking extra fine in that Lakers fit,” another said.

“PLEASE ROCK THE HEADBAND NEXT SEASON @lukadoncic,” a third added.

“MVP and Championship soon I can smell it,” a fourth wrote.

Headband Luka 

📸 via @lukadoncic pic.twitter.com/zDKH45sd0p

— Los Angeles Lakers (@Lakers) July 31, 2026

The Lakers will want a healthy Doncic who has made any possible changes to stay healthy.

He has been injured during his time with the Lakers, and with his physical style of play, he needs to handle wear and tear better.

Additionally, any additional lateral movement would be game-changing, unlocking an ability to put his size to use and defend at a level better than normal.

If he can stay healthy and tick his defense up a bit, Doncic will be an MVP, even with all of the other elite players in his era.
