title: ‘We didn’t feel safe’: Booking.com users face battle to get money back
description:
From melted electric sockets to shabby alternatives, readers tell of dealings with platform when things go wrong
Jane Ripley* spent some time researching the best apartment to stay in for her family’s trip to Batumi in Georgia, eventually settling on one with an “exceptional” rating on Booking.com.
But when the Ripleys arrived at 11pm on the first day, they were directed to another property that was shabby and had stains on the furniture and ceiling.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
From melted electric sockets to shabby alternatives, readers tell of dealings with platform when things go wrong

Jane Ripley* spent some time researching the best apartment to stay in for her family’s trip to Batumi in Georgia, eventually settling on one with an “exceptional” rating on Booking.com.

But when the Ripleys arrived at 11pm on the first day, they were directed to another property that was shabby and had stains on the furniture and ceiling.

“The host was unfriendly … We had genuine concerns about raising complaints directly. We were forced to find and pay for alternative accommodation for the remaining four nights at a further cost of £334,” she says.

Ripley made a series of complaints, starting the day after they arrived at the property. She says the property has since been removed from the site, but despite asking for a full refund of £570 for the original booking and the replacement accommodation, she has been offered only £36 in credits.

She is one of a number of readers who have contacted Guardian Money with stories of trying to get their money back after booking with the travel platform.

Millions of people use accommodation platforms such as Booking.com, Airbnb and Vrbo each year without a hitch, but when things go wrong, the sites’ terms and conditions suggest the companies have no liability for compensating people.

This remains a grey area in law – and holidaymakers are ending up out of pocket as a result.

If you have difficulties with your hotel when you book a package deal, you will be covered financially and legally by the Package Travel and Linked Travel Arrangements Regulations 2018, which means the holiday operator is responsible for sorting out any problems – from disruption caused by wildfires to the hotel not being up to scratch.

But if you book accommodation through Booking.com, the terms state that the contract is between you and the host. “When you make (or request) a booking, it’s directly with the service provider – we’re not a ‘contractual party’,” say the terms and conditions.

As a result, getting compensation or your money back is not as clearcut.

It is a similar story when booking with Airbnb, according to its terms and conditions. And also Vrbo, which says agreements are between guests and the travel providers. “We are not a party to any such agreements,” it says.

The consumer campaigner Martyn James says that by stating they are not part of the contract, these companies can argue they are only acting as a conduit and are not responsible for the supply of goods or services.

“This hasn’t really been tested in law massively, but I’d be willing to bet that the courts would take a dim view of the businesses operating in these grey areas,” he says

Travellers who have contacted Guardian Money have been frustrated by Booking.com’s inability to force hosts to pay up.

Before arriving at a hotel he had booked in Mongolia, John Taylor* was charged £1,177 – £120 more than the agreed price. When he cancelled, there was no refund, he says, even though free cancellation was part of the booking.

After “rounds of chasing” and giving Booking.com evidence of the payment, he was told by the website he was entitled to a refund but that the hotel had not engaged with Booking.com. He had still not received a refund when he contacted the Guardian in April. It eventually arrived in the middle of June.

Another reader, Kate Worthing*, booked a Parisian apartment for a weekend last summer. It was described as having an “elegant and refined” location. But the apartment building was in the middle of a refurbishment, with uncovered electrical wires in the communal hallway, and there were automatic lights that did not function. The rental itself contained worn fixtures and fittings and a melted electrical socket, she says.

“The main reason we left was because we didn’t feel safe. The electrical faults and wooden staircase, with no discernible fire escape, were not an option, and we were not prepared to put our family at risk,” she says. When she managed to contact the host, she was refused a refund of the £1,700 she had paid, as they claimed it was safe.

Booking.com told her that it “facilitates reservations between guests and accommodation partners, and in refund matters we are bound by the property’s policies and their final decision on waiving fees”.

It said it could not issue a full refund but offered £417 in travel credits as compensation.

Guardian Money contacted Booking.com about these and other cases. It said the hotel or apartment owner is responsible for providing refunds if something goes awry.

“We’d expect our accommodation partners to be on hand for guests during their stay, but if there is an issue at check-in, customers should contact us as soon as possible,” it said.

“As well as relocations, we can also advocate on their behalf and raise issues directly with the accommodation provider, and work to reach a resolution. If there are repeated issues with a property, we can and will address these with the accommodation owner to ensure future guests have a good experience.”

For travellers worried about being caught in the gap between a platform and a host, James says people should try to book directly with the provider, but use caution.

“I use these [aggregator] sites to compare and contrast, then look into booking direct,” he says. “If you call the hotel, you might even get a discount from them for doing so. Watch out for private apartments, though. This is where fakes have lurked, and any firm that asks you to pay by bank transfer knows that you can’t recall the money if things go wrong.”

title: 'What a weekend for the Nairne family' - sister inspires brother to judo gold
description: Ethan Nairne defeats his compatriot Benjamin Levy in an all-English men's -73kg final to win gold at the Commonwealth Games.
fullText:
Ethan Nairne defeated his compatriot Benjamin Levy in an all-English men's -73kg final to win judo gold at the Commonwealth Games, while Kelly Petersen-Pollard became the women's -70kg champion.

Nairne beat Scotland's Daniel Pacitti, Wales' Ben Moore and the Gambia's Faye Njie on his way to the final at the SEC Centre.

He had to be patient against Levy but a one-armed shoulder throw eventually clinched gold by Yuko.

The 24-year-old was joined on the podium by Levy and Northern Ireland's Josh Green, who claimed bronze with a golden score victory over Welshman Moore.

It is a second Commonwealth Games medal for the Nairne family this week after Lele, Ethan's older sister, won bronze by ippon with an emphatic throw to the mat to defeat Ghanas Frema Agyei within just 28 seconds on Friday.

"What a weekend it's been for the Nairne family," he said. "Her getting bronze spurred me on even more. It motivated me to go out there and do my best."

England's Kelly Petersen-Pollard, a bronze medallist in 2022, claimed gold in Glasgow as Australia's Aoife Coughlan was disqualified in the final when she picked up a third penalty in the golden score period.

"Literally four weeks ago she beat me on penalties and now, it's me! It's so nice," she said. "This is such a nice feeling. I'm buzzing."

Jemima Yeats-Brown stepped on to the podium alongside Petersen-Pollard after she defeated New Zealand's Moira de Villiers with a decisive ippon after the match went to golden score.

"That was my last contest before I retire," she said. "I decided at the start of the year my body has been through enough. I wanted to finish on a high here and I have.

"I felt an edge today, I knew if this was it I needed to make a good run of it. I told my friends and family so I couldn't go back on it, I needed to finish strong."

England's Jamal Petgrave was unable to defend his -90kg title from Birmingham in four years ago, but secured the bronze by Waza-Ari as he brought down New Zealand's Noah Wallis.

title: St Helens misery continues as York seal memorable win
description: York Knights pile more misery on ailing St Helens with their first win over them in 80 years.
fullText:
Tries: Bennison, Field 2, Balmforth, Vaughan, Williams Goals: Bennison 5

Tries: Davies, Wright, Welsby 2, Robertson, Douglas Goals: Hastings 4

York Knights piled more misery on ailing St Helens with their first win over them in 80 years.

The teams went in level at 16-16 at the break with Jon Bennison, Oli Field and Denive Balmforth going over for the home side and Jake Davies, Shane Wright and Jack Welsby scoring tries for Saints.

Despite being a man down when Ata Hingano was sin-binned York went in front when veteran Paul Vaughan showed real grit to get the ball down and then Nikau Williams got over after the visitors failed to deal with a kick.

Welsby's superb second gave Saints hope but Field went in with eight minutes to go for his second and although late tries from Harry Robertson and Jacob Douglas set up a tense finish York held out.

St Helens boss Rowley leaves after less than a year

York sign Huddersfield's English on loan deal

St Helens prop Delaney out for the season

Ragged Saints, who are under the interim charge of Eamon O'Carroll for the rest of the season after Paul Rowley's exit last week, have lost eight of their past 12 matches.

The 10-time Super League winners remain in seventh place and are in real jeopardy of missing out on the play-offs for the first time.

The injury-hit away side had looked dead and buried when Field went in for his second try after a lovely offload from Jack Martin but the visitors were only a missed conversion from Tristan Sailor from taking the game to golden-point extra time.

Even then they had time for one last play but a forward pass brought it to an end and meant they lost to York for the first time since 6 April 1946.

The error-strewn tone of the game was set after just three minutes when York failed to deal with a high kick from Jackson Hastings and Davies snaffled the loose ball to put the away team in front.

Ex-Saints man Bennison and then Field were beneficiaries of penalties to put the home side ahead only for another handling error to let Wright in and then Welsby avoided a last ditch tackle as O'Carroll's men went back in front.

Balmforth went in from dummy half to level the scores at 16 apiece at the break but Mark Applegarth's side's hopes were dealt a blow when Hingano was sin-binned for a high tackle.

However, Vaughan showed his experience and class to get over and Williams scrambled to touch the ball down when Saints erred on a kick as York went 12 ahead.

Welsby's super off-the-cuff score was the try of the match as they went the length of the field but his side could not avoid another damaging defeat.

York, who had lost to bottom-of-the-table Huddersfield last week, face a trip to Leigh on Friday while St Helens will bid to try and inject life into their season against lowly Hull FC on Thursday.

York Knights head coach Mark Applegarth told BBC Radio York:

"I would like to say I was nice and composed in the last minute or so but I was definitely a little twitchy.

"I'm really proud of how we showed the character to hang in there and grind out that win.

"I thought we made it a bit harder than we needed to in patches but that's one for Monday.

"It wasn't perfect but sometimes you've got find a way to win and we certainly did that."

St Helens interim coach Eamon O'Carroll told BBC Radio Merseyside:

"We didn't give in, which was great, but we certainly need to tidy a few things up in terms of our execution, more so defensively. When we got it wrong we got it wrong big.

"The yardage pens were very costly tonight.

"This is a much bigger job than just the performance at the weekend. This is about instilling some things that are going to help the club in the future, that is my main objective.

"There's still time yet and there's fight in the dog, definitely."

York: Mataafa, Galeano, Williams, Bennison, Hunter, McShane, Martin, Inman, Va'a, Foster, Field, Hingano, Djeukessi.

Interchanges: Balmforth, Vaughan, Thompson, Buchanan.

St Helens: Welsby, Murphy, Davies, Sailor, Douglas, Robertson, Hastings, Fifita, Burns, Walmsley, Wright, Host, Shorrocks.

title: Medic marks UFC's Serbia debut with 30-second win
description: Uros Medic puts on a statement performance to stop Daniel Rodriguez in just 30 seconds at the UFC's first event in Belgrade, Serbia.
fullText:
Uros Medic put on a statement performance to stop Daniel Rodriguez in just 30 seconds at the UFC's first event in Belgrade, Serbia.

Medic returned to his homeland for the first time in nine years, having moved to the United States to train, and sent a message to the rest of the welterweight division.

Rodriguez, 39, was fighting for the first time since spending eight months in a Mexican jail for possession of marijuana.

Medic, 33, dropped American Rodriguez with a left-right combination before forcing referee Jason Herzog to step in as he finished with kicks and punches on the canvas.

"It has been a really rough couple of weeks since I arrived home," Medic said.

"It didn't feel like home even though I was on home soil. Now we got the job done I just want to cry.

"I missed home so much - nine years is a long time. I left as a student at 22 years old with a dream and look where it got me."

It was Medic's fourth successive first-round victory and takes his overall record to 14 wins and three defeats.

Serbia became the 33rd country to host a UFC card and Medic rose to the occasion in front of a lively crowd on a record-breaking night.

Medic's TKO win took the overall tally on the card to a UFC-record 10 first-round finishes, with 12 finishes overall also a new high.

The number 14-ranked welterweight turned his attention to Birmingham's Leon Edwards and number-one contender Carlos Prates in the aftermath of a stunning victory.

"Carlos Prates is way ahead of me in the division but this would be a fight to remember," Medic said.

"I asked for Leon Edwards, I think he's still in hiding, but if he decides to come out of the hole he's shoved himself into then I'd be glad to knock him out."

Earlier, Wales' Oban Elliott slumped to a third successive loss against Brazilian debutant Michael Oliveira.

Elliott fell to the canvas when he was caught by a stiff left jab but quickly returned to his feet, before being dropped again by a right hook.

Oliveira sealed the win just shy of two minutes into the first round with ground and pound to extend his perfect professional record to 10 wins.

Elliott, 28, was seeking his first win since November 2024 and defeat puts his long-term future with the UFC in jeopardy.

He has three victories and three losses on his record since coming through Dana White's Contender Series to earn a contract.

title: Intensity, smiles & Lewandowski - inside Liverpool training under Iraola
description: Liverpool's pre-season under Andoni Iraola is ramping up - and here is what we learned from the first open training session under their new boss.
fullText:
As Liverpool's first open training session under Andoni Iraola began, Robert Lewandowski was taking penalties in the background.

The session took place at the performance centre of Major League Soccer side Chicago Fire, where the 37-year-old Pole now plays.

Under gloomy skies, Lewandowski blazed a spot-kick over the bar as Fire's training session came to an end and Iraola's got under way.

Here is what we learned from Liverpool's session.

Earlier this week, a video was posted on social media of Dominik Szoboszlai and Curtis Jones - who has been linked with a move to Inter Milan - having a heated argument at the end of Liverpool's win over Wrexham on Wednesday.

Asked about the situation on Thursday, Szoboszlai played it down, insisting all the players "were in the same boat" in terms of wanting the best for the club and each other.

Regardless, Szoboszlai, Jones and Kostas Tsimikas, who was also in the clip, walked out together in good spirits, doing keepy-uppies and joking with each other right in front of the cameras.

The argument was understood to be related to the fact that Szoboszlai had given Tsimikas the captain's armband instead of Jones but, by Friday, it seemed to have settled.

A little bit of passion is never a bad thing in an elite sporting environment but, with the way footage can be captured from anyone inside a stadium, sometimes it is better to keep things behind closed doors.

It was far from ideal - and it served as a reminder for Iraola that he must appoint a vice-captain soon, with the vacancy open after Andy Robertson's departure.

Record signing Alexander Isak also returned to Liverpool training this week.

He, Florian Wirtz and Ryan Gravenberch all missed the trip to New York, where Liverpool beat Wrexham 1-0 in their second pre-season fixture, but are expected to feature on Sunday against Leeds.

Jeremy Jacquet missed training but was in the gym as the club carefully manage his recovery from the shoulder injury he sustained in February.

The centre-back is a doubt for the weekend, despite Iraola suggesting earlier in the week that he would feature.

Joe Gomez, who has been ruled out for the start of the Premier League season, was also in the gym.

Once the warm-ups were done, the intensity in Iraola's drills was clear to see. He likes to get heavily involved and was particularly animated, using phrases like "play in possession" and "quicker, quicker" repeatedly.

There were celebrations between players whenever they scored in the mini-drills and the atmosphere was generally positive, with Iraola unafraid to step in and point out something, or discuss a player's position.

The squad then separated, with one group moving on to a smaller pitch for a nine-a-side match while another group worked on set-pieces with Iraola's assistants, Tommy Elphick and Shaun Cooper.

Wirtz was on corner duty, while Elphick even put on a bib to get involved.

"I just can say that the training is really fun, I enjoyed every training [session] until now," Wirtz told LFC TV after. "We play a lot of games and possessions, and that's exactly what I like. I just enjoyed it until now."

Liverpool's Jones argues with Szoboszlai after game

Watching on was Mike Gordon, the Fenway Sports Group president, who is now overseeing Liverpool operations again. He is expected to be at the game on Sunday at Soldier Field in Chicago.

Liverpool had a team dinner on Thursday evening, with Iraola sharing a drink with the likes of Phil Thompson and Robbie Fowler after.

Thompson told BBC Sport they spoke about a number of things, from the season ahead to their families.

Iraola wasn't even born when former defender Thompson won the third of his three European Cups for Liverpool. But this was a sign of the new head coach recognising the legends of the club and the weight they still carry.

Iraola still has three weeks before his first Premier League game as Liverpool manager - but the seeds of his tenure are getting planted here in the Windy City.

title: Chamberlain stuns O'Leary with knockout win in Dublin
description: Briton Mark Chamberlain stuns Republic of Ireland's Pierce O'Leary as he dropped him twice on the way to securing a knockout win in the 10th round to claim the IBO light-welterweight belt.
fullText:
Briton Mark Chamberlain stunned Republic of Ireland's Pierce O'Leary as he dropped him twice on the way to securing a knockout win in the 10th round to claim the IBO light-welterweight belt.

Chamberlain had to climb off the canvas himself in the seventh round as O'Leary struck him with a ferocious body shot in front of a capacity crowd in Dublin.

But just as momentum appeared to be swinging in the favour of O'Leary, Chamberlain found a breakthrough and managed to get the stoppage late on.

Portsmouth's Chamberlain now moves to 18 wins with one defeat, bouncing back to winning ways for the first time since losing to Josh Padley in 2024.

This was Chamberlain's first fight since he drew with Jack Rafferty in Altrincham last summer.

"First of all respect to Pierce for giving me this opportunity," Chamberlain told DAZN after the fight.

"I'm not a stranger to an away day and anyone that knows me knows that I will fight anyone and if that means that I have to go into the champions' back garden then I will do that.

"I've never been hurt before in a fight but that body shot stopped me in my tracks but fortunately I was able to get thorugh it and weather the storm.

"We've been working on new things in the gym and it's all paid off, I asked Frank (Warren) in the dressing room before the fight if we could bring a show down to Portsmouth, I'd love that. "

After a tight and cagey first round, Chamberlain stunned the home crowd of around 7,000 as he landed a flush left hand that sent O'Leary flying back onto the canvas.

Chamberlain then found another big shot in the next round as he sent his opponent to the floor again with a short left hook.

But O'Leary responded well to the knockdowns, rallied by his home crowd as he pressed on to find a way back into the fight.

He then found a breakthrough at the end of the seventh round as he backed Chamberlain into a corner and sent a punishing shot into his chest.

Chamberlain was slow to get to his feet but survived the count and managed to avoid major punishment before the bell sounded.

O'Leary continued to press on, with Chamberlain looking tired and the Irishman buoyed by the crowd.

But Chamberlain struck in the 10th with a combination that saw O'Leary drop his hands and then pressed on, landing a number of clean shots that included a straight right hand to send O'Leary tumbling into the ropes and to the canvas.

Fight promoter Frank Warren revealed after the fight that there is a rematch clause in the fight contract that could see the pair fight again in the near future.

British and Commonwealth super-featherweight champion Royston Barney-Smith beat fellow Briton Reece Bellotti in the chief support.

The 22-year-old from Southampton outclassed Bellotti across 10 rounds to pick up the vacant IBO intercontinental belt.

Bellotti took the fight to Barney-Smith, stalking down the southpaw and at times having success as he pushed him against the ropes and unloaded with dangerously intentioned shots.

But for the majority of the fight, Barney-Smith boxed smartly off the back foot, picking Bellotti apart with a variety of punches and manoeuvring a number of aggressive surges with some smart footwork.

The victory takes him to 17 wins without defeat since turning professional in 2022.

title: I can't believe I'm living this life - Finucane
description: Emma Finucane is the first Welsh woman to collect three golds at a single Commonwealth Games.
fullText:
Three nights at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome and three gold medals for Wales' cycling superstar.

Emma Finucane became the first Welsh woman to collect that haul at a single Commonwealth Games.

Just as it was on Friday, Finucane and Anna Morris stole the show, both topping the podium on the same night.

Team-mate Jess Roberts joined Morris on the podium in the points race by claiming silver, a feat matched by James Ball and pilot Matthew Rotherham in a dramatic men's tandem B sprint.

Wales have now won 10 cycling medals including five golds, three silvers and two bronze. Eight of those podium positions have been achieved by Welsh women.

Only Australia, with a population nearly nine times larger, sit above them in the track cycling medal standings.

Team Wales roll of honour at Commonwealth Games

The 1,000m time trial was making its debut at these Games and featured a mix of sprinters and endurance athletes for this halfway-house event.

Then came the woman from Carmarthen.

Buoyed by the crowds, Finucane set the pace, clocking one minute 05.285 seconds which guaranteed a bronze medal, with just two left to ride.

Neither England's Sophie Capewell nor New Zealand's Olympic sprint champion Ellesse Andrews were able to match that mark.

You'd imagine that winning a new event would require a lot of practice and a specific plan.

"It was the unknown," she said.

"I went into it not knowing what I could do because I'd never really done one before. I just had to hurt myself as much as I could, and I did.

"I'm not sure I'll be doing one of them again!"

It seems that there is nothing Finucane cannot do.

Only weightlifters David Morgan and Andy Phillips can match the 23-year-old's achievements at a single Games, when they both won three golds in Auckland in 1990.

And Finucane has one more race to come.

"I came into these Games wanting to win a gold," she said.

"To do it three times, I did not think would happen to me.

"I just can't believe I'm living this life at the moment. I've got one more event, so we'll just see what I can do."

Should Finucane repeat the feat in Sunday's women's keirin, she would become the most successful Welsh woman in Commonwealth Games history, taking the two-day old title of Para-athlete Olivia Breen.

The sprinting superstar has an endurance counterpart in team-mate Morris.

Once again at these Games the Welsh anthem reverberated around the velodrome twice in one night.

Prince Louis even got in on the act, donning a bucket hat with 'Beicio Cymru' - Welsh for Welsh Cycling - written on the front.

This time Morris had company on the podium, with Roberts stood beside her on the next step.

"This one was super cool," she said.

"We're team-mates and really close friends. We often room together, so to share that moment with her was just amazing."

The qualified doctor won gold on Friday and thought she had won silver too in the women's scratch event before she was relegated to fifth for entering the sprinter's lane when her opponent was already there.

There was no such bad luck today.

She bossed the race from start to finish and claimed her second gold.

“It felt like a hard race to be honest," said the World champion.

"It feels like a blur. I just know I was full gas to the line in that last sprint."

Roberts clung on to second, picking up two points on the last lap to hold off Australian bronze winner Georgia Baker, who was just one point back.

This was her first individual medal after collecting team pursuit bronze alongside Morris, Megan Barker and Ciara Oliva on Thursday.

"Incredible," she said, when asked how she was feeling.

"To get an individual medal as well, that makes it even more special.

"I'm so surprised but really happy."

Wales’ success on the track has not been without incident and tonight was no different.

On Thursday, 18-year-old Ioan Hepburn pulled out of the bronze medal race on the start line of the men’s team sprint with an illness.

We also had Morris’ silver success taken away when she was relegated off the podium on Friday.

Saturday saw drama in Ball’s men’s tandem B sprint final.

He and pilot Rotherham lost the first of three races to Neil Fachie and Aaron Pope when the home favourites caught them by surprise with an early attack.

The Welsh pair clawed their way back to force a decider.

After an unconventional start, where both flew out the gates, there was a coming together on the back strait which saw Fachie and Pope sprawled on the Serbian pine.

The raucous arena fell eerily quiet before they rose to their feet and dusted themselves off.

Battered and bruised, the Scots roared home in the restarted race, with Wales ruing what might have been.

“It's pretty raw right now, I'm not going to lie," said Ball.

"We knew we had a job to do. Obviously, we were buzzing off the second round win but it didn't go our way."

Pilot Matt Rotherham felt Wales were denied an opportunity.

"We took position one, we were in control of the race," said Rotherham.

"And then I feel like Scotland rode into us and knocked themselves off.

"To my mind, they caused the incident and we should get first choice of the position we want to be in when we come to the restart.

"We weren't given that opportunity.

"It's like all our advantage and all our tactical opportunity got taken away by no fault of our own and by the fault of our opponents."

A second crash of the night occurred in the evening's final race, the men's 10km scratch.

Several riders received treatment in the aftermath though Welshman Rhys Britton walked away relatively unscathed.

"I'm more disappointed than anything to be honest with you," he said.

"Just a few splinters and burns but I came off alright, my bike didn't come off that well.

"I think it was a good chance of a result and just a bit of wrong positioning just took me out of the race."

Fachie survives painful crash to take another gold after Wales 'poke bear'

Welsh Cycling had set an in-house target of seven medals prior to these Glasgow Games.

They have blown that out of the water.

They have accrued 10 medals, including five golds so far, with one more day of racing to come.

With Finucane and Morris set to ride again on Sunday, more medal success is no longer hope but expectation.

Wales at the Commonwealth Games

title: Nisbet leads from front as Aberdeen turn tables on Hearts
description: What a difference a year makes as Aberdeen get the better of Hearts - but what comes next for these two sides?
fullText:
What a difference a year makes.

Twelve months ago, Hearts came off a 100% record in the League Cup group stage to secure a home win over Scottish Cup winners Aberdeen, who had already sustained an early season European defeat.

On Saturday, Aberdeen were the home side, fresh from four straight League Cup wins and Premiership runners-up Hearts were smarting after a heavy aggregate Champions League qualifying loss to Sturm Graz.

Would it be the home side that prevailed again to set up a strong domestic charge? Yes, eventually - and, well it's too early to say.

The parallels with last season are compelling.

Hearts' challenge last term was led by a Scotland international forward in Lawrence Shankland, now skippering Rangers. Aberdeen are now captained by Kevin Nisbet and it was he who settled a dramatic evening at Pittodrie.

Aberdeen stun Hearts with incredible injury-time comeback win

Who has your Premiership club brought in & let go this summer?

Despite some early flurries from the Dons, Hearts seemed to be dealing calmly and confidently with their opponents and moved ahead through Oisin McEntee's close-range strike.

New players like Amadou Ba-Sy and Lauren Mendy integrated fairly seamlessly with experienced heads like captain-for-the-night Harry Milne and Blair Spittal. And there were chances for a second goal, with the final ball or shot often just the wrong choice.

All seemed well - until the 90th minute. Head coach Wouter Vrancken had urged his players to be more clinical in both boxes after 4-0 and 2-0 defeats by Sturm Graz in Champions League qualifying. They had partially addressed that with their goal but were undone defensively.

Podcast: Late drama at Pittodrie on Premiership opening weekend

Milne's booking-producing foul on Lewis Smith was the first real dent in Hearts' defensive resolve and Stuart Armstrong's free-kick delivery caused chaos. Dan Happe headed back across goal and Nisbet and Lewis Mayo raced in to apply the finish.

Mayo was eventually credited with the goal and Hearts' hopes of a VAR reprieve for any infringement were dashed.

And it got worse for the visitors as Stuart Findlay fouled the running figure of Toyosi Olusanya in the box, meaning a penalty and a red card for the Hearts defender. Nisbet may have been denied the first goal but he wasn't going to be denied again.

Now Vrancken faces the task of rousing his players for the arduous task of taking on the might of Portugal's Benfica in Europa League qualifying, with the first leg scheduled for Thursday in Lisbon (20:00 BST).

"We give it away in five minutes," was the Belgian's post-match response.

"We had to be smarter. We were going in attack with too many people there instead of keeping control and managing the counter, especially when you are 1-0 ahead.

"When the next game is on again, you have to switch again because you cannot go with these feelings again in the next game. We have to be ready and fully focused again."

Having taken over in March, Stephen Robinson had a couple of months' worth of competitive games to assess the Aberdeen squad before planning an assault on the transfer market.

Substantial change followed, with 12 players brought in, including a number of Premiership stalwarts, and a larger number leaving.

"If you're going to win a game, it's a good way to do it," Robinson commented wryly afterwards.

"We certainly showed the character and the fight that I didn't believe was here last year and certainly that was a real plus for me."

So what comes next? Can Aberdeen emulate Hearts' high-flying campaign of last season? As Robinson was keen to stress, it's early days.

"We have to remember it's one game," he said. "You take the criticism when you lose games so I think the players deserve a lot of credit for their mentality.

"It's a very good result. It's a start but that's all it is."

Former Aberdeen captain and manager Willie Miller:

To get a win from where they were - outstanding - but Hearts have got themselves to blame. Aberdeen have kept going right to the end. A sensational victory.

What a penalty it was. It's top quality, it's everything that should be about a penalty and how you deal with it. He had a long wait as well. He was calm, he was confident. It was a laser into the top corner.

Former Hearts midfielder Michael Stewart:

Hearts are being punished for recurring mistakes. They're not taking care of business.

The manager is an attacking type but he needs to get a balance. I was unsure on his substitutions. Why change the centre-halves? There's elements of the performance that they've been crucially punished for. These are recurring themes that are undermining any good work that's being done.

title: Woad & Hull in contention going into Open final round
description: England's Lottie Woad and Charley Hull are both in contention going into the final round of the AIG Women's Open at Royal Lytham and St Annes.
fullText:
-7 Y Noh (US); -4 E Henseleit (Ger), L Li (US), J Thitikul (Tha), Ryu (Kor), S Kuwaki (Jap); -3 L Woad (Eng)

Selected others: -2 C Hull (Eng); -1 L Ko (Nz); +1 N Korda (US), L Coughlin (US); +2 C Boutier (Fra), M Rhodes (Eng)

England's Lottie Woad and Charley Hull are both in contention heading into the final round of the AIG Women's Open at Royal Lytham and St Annes.

Woad carded a one-under 70 on Saturday to sit at three under while Hull recovered from three early bogeys to sign for a 71, leaving herself five shots behind leader Yealimi Noh, at two under overall.

"I was pretty proud," Hull told Sky Sports.

The 30-year-old, who is chasing her maiden major title after being a runner-up on five occasions, crucially made birdies on the 15th and 16th holes as she fought back on the back nine and then scrambled to save par on the penultimate hole.

"The first six holes I played like a 10 handicapper and I missed three putts I should have holed from inside five feet that would have kept me at level par instead of three over," Hull added.

"Then I did have a bit of a bounce-back. I was pretty happy with the way I finished."

On a day when the challenging windy conditions were again a feature on the Lancashire coast, American Noh was one of only nine players to end the third round under par as she climbed to the top of the leaderboard with a two-under 69.

However, a stellar cast that contains four of the top 10 players on the globe are within five shots and will aim to chase down the world number 69 in Sunday's fourth round.

Germany's Esther Henseleit, who fired a four-under 67 is three shots back at four under along with American Lucy Li, Japan's Shiho Kuwaki, world number two Jeeno Thitikul, of Thailand, and Friday's overnight leader South Korean Ryu Hae-ran, who is seeking her third consecutive major title.

New Zealand's three-time major winner Lydia Ko rolled in three birdies on the back nine to also remain in the mix at one under.

Meanwhile, world number one Nelly Korda's prospects of securing a career grand slam were dented by a double-bogey six on the 18th that leaves the American eight shots adrift of the lead.

On a moving day that delivered more ups and downs than the Big Dipper rollercoaster just down the road in Blackpool, the main focus for home fans as Saturday evening drew in was Hull's charge on the closing holes and Woad's continued ability to loiter towards the top of the leaderboard.

Woad, 22, who finished second in the Evian Championship just over 12 months ago as an amateur and ended up in a tie for 16th at the same event last month, delivered another promising display without ever quite getting her putter to run hot on the greens until the 16th hole.

"That back nine was playing very tough with that wind. Probably the strongest it's been all week and playing long, so definitely pars were good on that," said Woad.

"Then eventually I knew that 16 would be a good chance and I managed to capitalise on that."

Prior to that Ayaka Furue's sensational round of 65 which included an eagle on the par-five seventh had caught the eye alongside the performance of Henseleit, who went out in 31 and then set the clubhouse target as she steadily came home in par as the wind began to pick up.

And it was at that point that second-round leader Ryu went into reverse on the back nine.

Three birdies inside the opening six holes had given Ryu a healthy four-stroke advantage over the field.

Six holes later she was trailing by one after making her fifth bogey of the round and a further dropped shot on the 14th contributed to a disappointing three-over 74 on a day when she probably felt like she had spent time in each and every one of the 167 bunkers dotted around the famous course in the north west of England.

If one moment encapsulated her round, it was on the 10th when her approach found an almost unplayable spot in the sand.

For the second day running, Ryu deliberately chipped her ball a few feet into the middle of a bunker to provide an escape route with her next shot even if it cost her a stroke, that she later described as her "best" bogey of the day.

"[It was] just a tough day today," said Ryu.

"I know that [I] have won [majors] so it's not too stressful. Tomorrow the wind is supposed to be the same as today so I [will] just try keeping lower and [finding] no bunker[s]."

In contrast, Noh enjoyed a chip-in par save from the sand on the second and played a stunning shot out of a bunker on the 17th to save par.

However, having only won one event on the LPGA Tour since turning professional in 2019 and only finishing in the top 10 of a major once in that time, she will be in relatively unchartered territory when she gets under way in the final pairing on Sunday.

One omen in her favour is that no player has held a three-stroke lead after 54 holes of the Women's Open and failed to go on to win the championship.

title: Emotional Kerr delivers moment Glasgow 2026 has waited for
description: There were no pacers and no wave lights. This was a Saturday night scrap - Glasgow rules - and Josh Kerr wasn't going to let anyone beat him in that fight.
fullText:
There were no pacers. No wave lights. No declarations about what time he would run or what record he would beat. This was a Saturday night scrap - Glasgow rules - and Josh Kerr wasn't going to let anyone beat him in that fight.

Not his childhood pal and Scotland team-mate Jake Wightman. Not the Australian prodigy Cam Myers. Not the former Olympic silver medallist Timothy Cheruiyot.

This Commonwealth Games men's mile was his race, in his country, in front of his people. This gold medal really meant something.

Kerr's explosion of joy after he crossed the line and swaddled himself in a Saltire - having conducted the crowd during his final few strides - made that clear.

And so did his halting attempts to sing along with Flower of Scotland, the 28-year-old repeatedly stopping to bite his lip before wiping away tears from each eye.

"We rush through these moments so quickly," Kerr told BBC Sport Scotland, having spent the best part of 45 minutes doing selfies and signatures. "So I was just telling myself to slow down.

"In my head, I was flashing through all the hard moments and realising that I've come a long way. And to have Flower of Scotland playing versus the GB national anthem, it's just different. Not many times in my career I'll ever have that."

Kerr on why Commonwealth mile glory matters to him

Britain's Kerr breaks 27-year mile world record in London

When Kerr crossed the line, the clock showed he was almost eight seconds slower than when running the fastest time ever for the mile in London last month. Three minutes 54.12 seconds.

What it didn't show was that for three of the four laps, this was more rammy than race.

Emerging between fireworks, Kerr had strutted out on to the track, spinning a bottle, and allowed his 12 rivals to sprint away. Only once they checked and began to run back did he stretch his own legs and acknowledge the crowd. Aura.

The 28-year-old also made sure to position himself between Myers and Cheruiyot on the start line. A flex, perhaps, but why not? Kerr has the credentials, after all. Former world champion, Olympic silver and bronze, the big dog in this fight.

And he needed all of his snarl and bite to survive the three laps of jostling, barging and bumping that followed.

The race was slow, too slow. And physical, really physical. Could Kerr - trapped in the pack, pinned to the kerb - deal with that? "As long as you stay on your feet, it's fine," was his assessment afterwards.

At the time, Kerr gave his answer as the bell tolled. In a flash, he made his move, bursting to the outside in pursuit of Myers and Cheruiyot, who made theirs momentarily first.

With 250m to go, Kerr left them behind. Wightman gamely tried to follow but how do you chase down a man this fast? His brave gamble failed and the bronze medallist from the last two Games trailed home in sixth.

"I peeked up at the screen, saw I had a bit of a gap, and I felt great," added the Edinburgh athlete, who has been racing at Scotstoun since he was a child.

"I was just trying to stay present and enjoy it. I learned how to race on that track - and I've had some pretty bad ones out there - so to really enjoy that last 100m was a really important moment."

It was the moment Glasgow 2026 has been building to. The historic, reinstated, Blue Riband event of these Games got a fittingly elite winner. As a student of the sport's history, Kerr will appreciate that.

And as a kid who was at the athletics event at Hampden in 2014, he knew how much joy every man, women and child inside this place would derive from every picture he had taken, every word he shared with them, and every scrawl of his name.

"I have to take my time out there because they've waited and put their hard-earned money to come out and watch me perform," he said.

"You've got to stay in your lane and realise I'm lucky coming into this championship healthy, ready to go and I'm in the best shape of my life. And to do that in front of a home crowd is very special."

title: Root in 'very different place' over Test captaincy
description: England's Joe Root is ready to embrace his second stint as Test captain, saying he is in a "very different place" to when he stepped down from the role four years ago.
fullText:
England's Joe Root is ready to embrace his second stint as Test captain, saying he is in a "very different place" to when he stepped down from the role four years ago.

First appointed captain in 2017, Root led England in a record 64 Tests and oversaw a record 28 wins as skipper before stepping down in April 2022 following a 10-wicket defeat by West Indies.

At that time, England had won just one of their past 17 Tests, including a 4-0 Ashes humbling away in Australia, while also navigating Covid restrictions, with Root admitting the job "took its toll" on his health.

"It had become a very unhealthy relationship, the captaincy and me. I couldn't leave it at the ground any more, it was coming home," Root said in June 2022.

"As soon as I made the decision, I knew it was the right thing to do. I felt like a big weight had been lifted."

Root has sparkled since relinquishing the captaincy, averaging over 54 since June 2022 compared to an average of 46.44 in the five years prior and scoring 16 of his 41 Test centuries.

However, he told BBC Sport he had no doubts when he was offered the opportunity to return to the role by incoming head coach Stephen Fleming, adding the New Zealander's appointment was a big factor in his decision.

Sheffield-born Root, 35, will begin his second stint as full-time captain against Pakistan at Headingley on 19 August, with Fleming joining up with the team ahead of December's tour of South Africa.

"It's one of the greatest honours you could wish to have. I'm very excited by it," Root, who filled the role on an interim basis in June when then captain Ben Stokes missed the second Test against New Zealand following an incident at a nightclub, told BBC Sport.

"I'm in a very different place to the last time I did it with a team in a very different position."

Fleming new England Test coach with Root captain

England captaincy could be what Root needs - Vaughan

On Fleming, who, like Root, holds national records for matches and wins as Test captain, he added: "I've admired him from afar, first as a player and recently as a coach. To get the chance to work together is going to be great fun.

"Once I'd spoken to Stephen about it and saw his energy and excitement for it and saw we're very aligned on it, I got excited very quickly."

Root and Fleming inherit a side in disarray, with series defeats in Australia and at home by New Zealand - which brought criticism of England's carefree playing style - coupled with a run of off-field disciplinary issues bringing the Bazball era to a disappointing conclusion when captain Stokes retired in June and coach Brendon McCullum was sacked a fortnight later.

The duo had previously overseen a resurgence in the Test side, winning 10 of their first 11 matches, and Root hopes he and Fleming can take inspiration from their tenure, rather than starting from scratch.

"Hopefully we can work and build on a lot of the good things that have happened over the last four years," Root said.

"I think Brendon and Ben did a brilliant job, in many ways, of turning things around and getting us in a position where hopefully now we can carry that forward in a slightly different way."

Expanding on his approach to his second captaincy in an in-house interview with the England & Wales Cricket Board, Root said: "The last four years have been the most fun I've had in professional cricket and a big part of that was down to the way they [McCullum and Stokes] got me to see the game.

"Clearly, the last little while is probably what's fresh in everyone's mind but you're looking at a four-year period where we did a lot of amazing things. I've taken a lot from that and I feel it will be a big part of how I want to approach things moving forward as a leader of this team.

"The thing that stands out the most for me is the shift in mindset that was created around how we want to play the game - trying to strip the fear away from things, make sure guys feel that they can really just allow their talent to come out as frequently as possible and in big moments in games. The more that can happen, the better.

"If we can do that alongside recognising when the right time is to put pressure back on teams, or when the right time is to soak it up and to maybe play situations slightly differently, become a little bit smarter in certain areas, then I think we'll be a very formidable team and a very difficult team to break down and to beat."

title: Shittu 'robbed' - are AI boxing judges the answer?
description: After commentators claim England's Dimeji Shittu was "robbed" in the Commonwealth Games final, is judging helped by artificial intelligence the answer?
fullText:
The pundits made their feelings known.

"Shocking. Terrible. Totally robbed," said former champion Richie Woodhall.

England's Dimeji Shittu had to settle for silver at the Commonwealth Games on Saturday after a controversial defeat by India's Ankush Panghal.

Shittu, 24, was docked a point in both the second and third rounds but even without that, he would not have won after more controversial decision-making.

"The referee has cost Shittu the contest," Woodhall said on TNT Sports. "He has been robbed. I really feel for him."

It meant one of boxing's oldest talking points - how it is officiated - reared its head again. Would judging run or supported by artificial intelligence help solve this problem?

Shittu was well-placed in his final after winning the round on all five of the judges' scorecards. One punch resulted in Ankush receiving a standing count.

The contest swung in the second round, however.

Despite Shittu appearing to land the majority of the blows, three of the judges gave the round to Ankush.

It meant when a point was harshly deducted for dipping his head low, the Englishman was trailing overall.

Then when Shittu was punished for the same offence again despite hurting Ankush through the final round, the contest was effectively decided.

"Do me a favour, referee," said Woodhall as the second penalty was given.

"That is dreadful, absolutely dreadful," said TNT commentator Dave Farrar.

Remarkably, four of the judges still gave the final round to Ankush which meant the point deductions did not even matter. Shittu would have lost without them.

"How did [Ankush] win that last round on the scores 4-1?" Woodhall said.

"Absolutely terrible. Shocking. That is not sour grapes."

Shittu, to his credit, refused to get drawn into the debate afterwards.

He appeared distraught as the result was confirmed but said "whatever the referee says goes".

"A lot of people might say this about the referee, the judging, but at the end of the day I can only blame myself," he told BBC Sport.

"Those are the rules. We live and we learn.

"At the end of the day, it's a foul in amateur boxing. It cost me the fight.

"If people think I should have got the decision, fair play, I understand.

"But if I'm sitting here blaming judges, blaming refs, I'm not going to get better."

Delicious Orie, England's superheavyweight champion from the 2022 Commonwealth Games, was another who believed the result was unfair.

"The referee has stripped the medal from Dimeji," he told TNT Sports.

And Orie went on to suggest introducing AI into boxing judging would be a way to improve the situation.

The topic has been discussed increasingly in recent years with the technology being used to judge Tyson Fury's bout with Oleksandr Usyk, external behind the scenes in 2024.

Under president and former unified world champion Gennadiy Golovkin, World Boxing, which runs amateur boxing around the world including at the Olympics and Commonwealth Games, has made moves to look into the implementation.

Nothing is imminent but the desire is there to investigate whether AI it could help improve transparency and integrity.

Traditionalists, though, may feel that subjectivity is simply part of the sport.

Technology has been used in other sports but more often for factual situation – was a forward offside, did a forehand land out, was there an edge of a cricket bat?

Would AI be able to determine the power of a punch? Are all punches equal? Those are issues that need to be considered.

"I wouldn't necessarily be against it," Orie said.

"Then it becomes an objective sport. If I knew there was a specific set of scoring then yeah, bring AI.

"I would follow that rule book rather than someone's opinion."

title: Sawyers puts heartbreak behind her to claim gold
description: English long jumper Jazmin Sawyers overcomes previous major championship disappointments to win Commonwealth gold.
fullText:
England's Jazmin Sawyers was finally able to put previous disappointments at major championships behind her by winning the women's long jump at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

The 32-year-old bounced back from serious injury to celebrate a gold medal on a night when there was a silver for England's mixed 4x400m relay team and a bronze for pole vaulter Owen Heard.

Sawyers finished just outside the medals in fourth place at the previous games in Birmingham four years ago, failed to qualify for the final of the 2023 World Championships and was then forced to miss the 2024 Olympics.

She had to undergo surgery after rupturing her Achilles tendon on her take-off leg and so, rather than competing in Paris ended up commentating for the BBC.

But the Stoke-on-Trent born athlete put all those setbacks behind her on a memorable evening at Scotstoun with her fourth jump of 6.93m proving to be enough to claim the gold medal ahead of Nigeria's Ruth Usoro (6.87m) and Brooke BuschKuehl of Australia (6.80m).

"It hasn't properly hit me how this is the thing I've been telling myself all the horrible bits are for," she said.

"The feeling is overwhelming. I will do the horrible bits 100 times over, I'll do it and do it and do it. This is amazing."

Sawyers will now turn her attention to competing for Great Britain at the European Championships in Birmingham, which start on 10 August, but is keen to hang on to the memories Glasgow has given her.

"Twelve years ago almost to the day, I won a silver here in Glasgow (2014 Commonwealth Games) at my first major championships. It was a shock silver and I've held Glasgow close to my heart ever since," she added.

"It was the start of my career and so sensational and I had the time of my life. I take that as one of the best moments of my entire career, but when you've done that there's only one thing to do which is to upgrade."

A superb anchor leg from Lina Nielsen helped England to a silver medal in the mixed 4x400m relay in Glasgow.

It looked as though England could miss out on the medals altogether as they completed the final changeover with Nigeria's Ella Onojuvwevwo well in front.

But Onojuvwevwo finished third as she tired down the final 100m and was reeled back in by eventual gold medallists Jamaica and England's Nielsen.

"We knew the Nigerians and Jamiacans would be big threats," said Nielsen.

"The crowd got me going for the last 70 or 80 metres - my 400 metres have really improved this year and I trusted my training."

Owen Heard jumped just one centimetre short of his personal best to secure a bronze medal for England in the men's pole vault.

The 24-year-old finished in fifth place on his Commonwealth Games debut in 2022 but showed an impressive level of improvement as he came third with an effort of 5.70m.

Gold medallist Kurtis Marschall of Australia set a new games record with 5.85m while South Africa's Kyle Rademeyer took the silver, reaching the same 5.70m mark as Heard but finishing ahead of the Englishman on countback.

"I was in silver then bronze then nearly cleared a PB to go back up to silver," said Heard.

"It was a really good standard of competition, maybe even the best standard of Commonwealth pole vault ever. Me and the boys we put on a good show."

He will now make his Great Britain debut at the European Championships.
